a: Syphilis is caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema pallidum. Primary syphilis presents as a painless hard ulcer/chancre on external genitalia, mouth, or cervix.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Why can antibiotic medications (like penicillin) cure syphilis but have NO effect against AIDS?
a: Antibiotics specifically disrupt bacterial cell wall synthesis or bacterial ribosomes. Viruses (like HIV) lack cell walls, have no independent metabolic machinery, and replicate inside host cells, making them completely immune to antibiotics.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Define the genetics terms 'homozygous' and 'recessive'.
a: Homozygous individuals have two copies of the same allele (e.g. BB or bb). A recessive allele is masked in the presence of a dominant allele and only produces its phenotype when homozygous (bb).
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: A homozygous black-haired mouse (BB) is crossed with a homozygous brown-haired mouse (bb). All offspring are black. Which is the dominant hair colour?
a: When crossing true-breeding black and brown mice, all F1 offspring express black fur, proving the black allele (B) is dominant over the brown allele (b).
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: One of the heterozygous black mice (Bb) is bred with a homozygous brown mouse (bb). What is the expected phenotypic ratio among the offspring?
a: Punnett cross Bb × bb gives gametes B, b from one parent and b, b from the other: genotypes 50% Bb (black) and 50% bb (brown), a 1:1 ratio.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Which type of cell division halves the chromosome number from diploid to haploid, producing four genetically varied gametes?
a: Meiosis is the reduction division occurring in the gonads (testes and ovaries) that halves chromosome number and introduces genetic variation into gametes.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: In a family pedigree for phenylketonuria (PKU), two unaffected parents have a child with PKU. Is the PKU allele dominant or recessive, and why?
a: If unaffected parents produce an affected child, the allele must be recessive (parents are heterozygous carriers Hh; the child inherits hh). If dominant, at least one parent would have to show PKU.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: If parents are both heterozygous carriers of the PKU allele (Hh × Hh), what are the possible genotypes of an unaffected sibling?
a: An unaffected sibling does not have the genotype hh, so they can be either homozygous normal (HH, 1/3 probability) or a heterozygous carrier (Hh, 2/3 probability).
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: How does a down feather differ structurally and functionally from a flight feather on a bird?
a: Down feathers form a dense, fluffy underlayer close to the skin. Their barbs do not interlock, creating pockets of still trapped air that provide excellent thermal insulation in cold climates.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f). What is the genotype of a healthy carrier of cystic fibrosis?
a: A carrier possesses one normal dominant allele (F) and one mutated recessive allele (f), represented by the heterozygous genotype Ff.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Can a man homozygous for the normal allele (FF) and a woman who is a carrier (Ff) produce a child with cystic fibrosis (ff)?
a: Cross FF × Ff yields 50% FF (normal) and 50% Ff (healthy carriers). None of the offspring can be ff, so zero children will suffer from cystic fibrosis.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: How does the accumulation of thick, sticky mucus harm a person suffering from cystic fibrosis?
a: Defective chloride transport leads to dehydrated mucus. In the lungs, thick mucus clogs airways and traps pathogens. In the pancreas, it blocks enzyme ducts, causing malabsorption and weight loss.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: What is the shape of an abnormal red blood cell from a sufferer of sickle cell anaemia under low oxygen conditions?
a: Under low oxygen tension, abnormal haemoglobin (HbS) polymerises into rigid crystalline rods, distorting the red blood cell into a rigid, fragile sickle or crescent shape.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: What is the genotype of a person with the sickle cell trait (heterozygous carrier)?
a: Because the normal haemoglobin allele (HA) and the sickle haemoglobin allele (HS) are codominant, the heterozygous carrier genotype is written as HA HS.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Which genotype provides the greatest natural protection against severe malaria in tropical regions?
a: Individuals heterozygous for sickle cell (HA HS) enjoy the 'heterozygote advantage': the malaria parasite Plasmodium cannot multiply effectively in red cells containing HbS, granting resistance against fatal malaria.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: A man suffering from sickle cell anaemia (HS HS) marries a woman who is a carrier (HA HS). What percentage of their children is predicted to suffer from sickle cell anaemia?
a: The cross is HS HS × HA HS. The father provides only HS gametes; the mother provides 50% HA and 50% HS. Offspring: 50% HA HS (carriers) and 50% HS HS (sufferers).
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: What is the term for the process where individual organisms with characteristics best suited to their environment survive, reproduce, and pass on advantageous alleles?
a: Natural selection is the mechanism of evolution: individuals possessing advantageous phenotypic traits have higher reproductive fitness, increasing favorable allele frequencies over generations.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Using a dichotomous key for arthropods, which disease-carrying insect has wings shorter than its abdomen?
a: In the 0610 dichotomous key: wings present → wings shorter than abdomen identifies the Anopheles mosquito; wings longer than abdomen identifies the housefly (Musca).
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Which disease vector is an arachnid possessing four pairs of legs and no wings?
a: Ticks such as Ornithodorus belong to the class Arachnida. Adults have 4 pairs of jointed legs (8 legs), lack wings, and have no antennae.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: In the binomial naming system for the lion, Panthera leo, what do the two names represent?
a: Under the Linnaean binomial system, the first word represents the Genus (capitalized) and the second word represents the specific epithet or species (lowercase).
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: State two structural features that distinguish bacteria from viruses.
a: Bacteria are cellular organisms with peptidoglycan walls, cell membranes, cytoplasm, and ribosomes that reproduce independently. Viruses consist solely of a DNA/RNA core in a protein capsid and cannot reproduce outside host cells.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: State two features that distinguish arachnids (e.g. spiders) from crustaceans (e.g. crabs).
a: Arachnids have 8 legs (4 pairs), chelicerae, simple eyes, and zero antennae. Crustaceans have 10+ legs (5+ pairs), 2 pairs of antennae, compound eyes, and a calcified exoskeleton/carapace.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Which characteristics distinguish monocotyledonous plants from dicotyledonous plants?
a: Monocots possess a single seed leaf, parallel venation, floral organs in multiples of three, and fibrous roots. Dicots possess two seed leaves, branching reticulate venation, floral parts in 4s or 5s, and a taproot.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Why are fungi classified into their own distinct kingdom rather than being grouped with plants?
a: Fungi are heterotrophic saprophytes or parasites that do not contain chloroplasts or synthesize chlorophyll. Their cell walls are composed of chitin, whereas plant walls are composed of cellulose.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: State two structural features of insects that have contributed to their immense evolutionary success across diverse habitats.
a: Wings enable flight to locate food, find mates, and escape predators. The waterproof, waxy, chitinous cuticle prevents water loss in terrestrial and arid habitats, while high reproductive fecundity ensures rapid adaptation.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Which anatomical feature is unique to birds and distinguishes them from all other vertebrate classes?
a: Feathers are unique to the class Aves (birds). Other classes share endothermy (mammals) or egg laying (reptiles, amphibians, fish), but only birds possess feathers.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: In the nitrogen cycle, which group of bacteria lives in the root nodules of leguminous plants and converts atmospheric N2 into ammonium?
a: Symbiotic nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium) colonize root nodules of legumes, reducing atmospheric N2 gas into ammonium compounds used by the plant to synthesize proteins.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: What is the role of nitrifying bacteria in the soil nitrogen cycle?
a: Nitrifying bacteria are chemosynthetic aerobes: Nitrosomonas oxidizes ammonium ions into nitrites, and Nitrobacter oxidizes nitrites into nitrates, the form most readily absorbed by plant roots.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: If grassland is converted into farmland and maize is grown continuously year after year without fertiliser, what happens to soil nitrates and crop yield?
a: When crops are harvested and removed, plant biomass is no longer returned to the soil for decay and nitrification. Soil nitrates are progressively exhausted, leading to stunted crops and declining yields.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: How can a farmer maintain high crop yields without relying exclusively on expensive synthetic chemical fertilisers?
a: Organic manure and compost return decaying biomass to soil. Growing legumes (beans, groundnuts, clover) in rotation enriches soil nitrates naturally through symbiotic nitrogen fixation.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: In a freshwater pond food web, what is the trophic level of microscopic photosynthetic algae?
a: Algae and phytoplankton are photosynthetic autotrophs that trap light energy and manufacture organic matter, occupying the first trophic level as producers.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Why are food chains in nature typically limited to only four or five trophic levels?
a: Due to the second law of thermodynamics, roughly 90% of energy is dissipated as metabolic heat or lost in excretion/uneaten parts. By the 4th or 5th trophic level, remaining energy is insufficient to sustain a viable population.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: In a sigmoid (S-shaped) population growth curve, what causes the population to transition from exponential growth into a stationary plateau?
a: As population density nears the habitat's carrying capacity, density-dependent limiting factors (competition for food, shelter, disease, accumulation of waste) increase the death rate until births equal deaths.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Why has the global human population continued to grow exponentially rather than leveling off at a natural carrying capacity plateau?
a: Human technological innovation (sanitation, antibiotics, immunizations, synthetic fertilizers, global food distribution, disease control) has overcome natural limiting factors and lowered infant and adult mortality worldwide.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: In an African savanna food web, what immediate effect is expected on the water buffalo population if a massive grasshopper swarm consumes most of the grass?
a: Water buffalo are herbivorous grazers that depend directly on grass. Competition from a massive swarm of grasshoppers severely reduces food availability, resulting in starvation and population decline.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Why are isolated oceanic islands like South Uist easily colonized by birds but rarely colonized by non-flying mammals?
a: Flight enables birds to cross wide stretches of open sea and establish breeding populations on isolated islands. Non-volant terrestrial mammals are blocked by marine barriers.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Why did the introduction of hedgehogs onto South Uist island threaten native ground-nesting Corncrake birds with extinction?
a: Corncrakes nest directly on the ground in hayfields. Introduced hedgehogs have few natural island predators and prey heavily on unprotected bird eggs and chicks, while competing for invertebrate food.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: State two effective conservation measures to prevent the extinction of endangered ground-nesting birds on islands invaded by non-native predators.
a: Key conservation strategies include systematic eradication/removal of alien predators, creating fenced predator-proof breeding sanctuaries, delayed mowing practices, and captive breeding.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: What is the initial trigger in the process of aquatic eutrophication when untreated sewage or fertilizer enters a freshwater lake?
a: High concentrations of dissolved nitrates and phosphates act as limiting nutrients, sparking rapid, explosive growth of phytoplankton and filamentous algae across the lake surface (algal bloom).
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Why do submerged aquatic plants die during a severe algal bloom in a eutrophic lake?
a: The dense green layer of surface algae absorbs and reflects incoming sunlight. Light cannot penetrate to deeper water, so benthic and submerged aquatic vegetation cannot photosynthesize and dies.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Why do dissolved oxygen levels drop drastically to near zero during the advanced stages of eutrophication?
a: Masses of dead algae and submerged plants provide a vast organic substrate for saprophytic bacteria. These aerobic decomposers multiply rapidly and consume dissolved oxygen in respiration, creating fatal hypoxic/anoxic conditions.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: What is the primary physical process carried out in the first screening stage of modern sewage treatment?
a: The primary screening stage relies on coarse metal grates and fine screens to mechanically filter out large, non-biodegradable debris that would otherwise clog pumps and treatment channels.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: What biological process takes place in the aeration tanks (or trickling filters) during secondary sewage treatment?
a: In trickling filter beds or activated sludge aeration tanks, air is continuously supplied so colonies of aerobic bacteria, fungi, and protoctists can oxidize dissolved organic wastes into CO2, water, and harmless mineral ions.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Why is the final clear water effluent treated with chlorine gas or ultraviolet (UV) irradiation before discharge into natural waterways?
a: Chlorination or UV disinfection is the tertiary treatment step that destroys waterborne pathogens (e.g. Vibrio cholerae, Salmonella typhi, viral enteroviruses) before effluent is released into rivers or reservoirs.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: State two morphological leaf adaptations of xerophytic desert plants that minimise transpirational water loss.
a: Xerophytes have a thick impermeable waxy cuticle that blocks evaporation, and stomata sunken in pits or hair-lined grooves that trap humid air, reducing the diffusion gradient and minimizing transpiration.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Why do desert cacti have leaves reduced to sharp spines?
a: Modifying leaves into spines drastically reduces surface area where water could be lost by transpiration, while stem tissues take over photosynthesis and store water. Spines also protect against grazing animals.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: How does the extensive root system of desert xerophytes aid survival in arid environments?
a: Desert xerophytes exhibit dual root strategies: long penetrating taproots reach deep water reserves, while wide-spreading shallow root networks immediately capture rainfall from sudden desert showers before surface evaporation occurs.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Past Paper Bank

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the characteristics used to classify a thing as a living organism?
a: The characteristics of living organisms are commonly remembered as MRS GREN (Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition). Colour is not one of these characteristics.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The scientific naming system in which every organism is given a two-part Latin name is called:
a: Binomial nomenclature gives each organism a two-part name consisting of its genus and species, e.g. Homo sapiens.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which group of organisms is characterised by having a body made of thread-like hyphae and reproducing by spores, and cannot photosynthesise?
a: Fungi have a body made of hyphae (forming a mycelium), reproduce by spores, and obtain nutrients by absorption rather than photosynthesis.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A dichotomous key is used mainly to:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** identify an unknown organism through a series of paired choices

A dichotomous key identifies organisms by presenting a series of paired (either/or) statements about observable features, leading step by step to the correct identification.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Viruses are generally considered non-living because they:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** cannot reproduce independently outside a host cell

Viruses lack the cellular machinery to carry out life processes such as reproduction on their own; they can only replicate by hijacking a living host cell.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which kingdom includes organisms that are unicellular, lack a true nucleus, and have a cell wall made of peptidoglycan?
a: Bacteria are prokaryotes: unicellular organisms without a membrane-bound nucleus, with a cell wall containing peptidoglycan.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which of the following best describes 'sensitivity' as a characteristic of living organisms?
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** The ability to detect and respond to changes in the environment

Sensitivity (irritability) is the ability of an organism to detect and respond appropriately to stimuli/changes in its surroundings.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The organelle responsible for controlling the activities of a cell and containing hereditary material is the:
a: The nucleus contains the cell's DNA (hereditary material) and controls the cell's activities, including growth and reproduction.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which structure is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
a: Plant cells have a rigid cellulose cell wall outside the cell membrane, which gives support and shape; animal cells lack this structure.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The site of aerobic respiration, where most ATP is produced, is the:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** mitochondrion

Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, producing most of a cell's ATP (energy currency).
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which organelle is responsible for photosynthesis in plant cells?
a: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy used to carry out photosynthesis.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A large, fluid-filled space in a plant cell that helps maintain turgidity is the:
a: The large permanent vacuole in plant cells is filled with cell sap and helps maintain turgor pressure, keeping the cell firm.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Root hair cells are specialised for water absorption mainly by having:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** a long, thin extension increasing surface area

Root hair cells have a long, thin projection that greatly increases surface area in contact with soil water, maximising water absorption by osmosis.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Red blood cells are adapted for oxygen transport by:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** having no nucleus, allowing more space for haemoglobin

Mature red blood cells lack a nucleus, providing more internal space to pack in haemoglobin, which binds and carries oxygen.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The movement of molecules from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration is called:
a: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Osmosis is best defined as the movement of:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** water from a region of high water potential to low water potential through a partially permeable membrane

Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: When a plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution, it will most likely become:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** plasmolysed

In a concentrated (hypertonic) solution, water leaves the cell by osmosis, causing the cell membrane to pull away from the cell wall - a condition called plasmolysis.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Active transport differs from diffusion because active transport:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** requires energy (ATP) and can move substances against a concentration gradient

Active transport uses energy from respiration (ATP) to move substances from a region of low concentration to high concentration, against the concentration gradient.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Root hair cells absorb mineral ions from the soil mainly by:
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** active transport, since minerals are often more concentrated inside the root hair cell

Mineral ions are often at a lower concentration in the soil than inside root hair cells, so active transport (requiring energy) is used to absorb them against the concentration gradient.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A red blood cell placed in distilled (pure) water will most likely:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** swell and possibly burst (haemolysis)

Distilled water has a higher water potential than the cell's cytoplasm, so water enters the cell by osmosis; since animal cells lack a cell wall, they can swell and burst (haemolysis).
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which cell structure controls what enters and leaves a cell?
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** Cell membrane

The cell (plasma) membrane is partially permeable and controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A tissue is best defined as:
a: A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to carry out a particular function, such as muscle tissue or xylem tissue.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: An organ is best defined as:
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** a group of different tissues working together to perform a specific function

An organ is made up of two or more different tissues working together to carry out a specific function, such as the heart or a leaf.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which of the following elements is found in proteins but NOT in carbohydrates or fats?
a: Proteins contain nitrogen (in their amino acid groups) in addition to carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, which distinguishes them from carbohydrates and fats.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The building blocks (monomers) of proteins are called:
a: Proteins are made up of long chains of amino acids joined together by peptide bonds.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The test used to detect the presence of starch in a food sample uses:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** Iodine solution, turning blue-black

Iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black in the presence of starch.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which test is used to detect the presence of reducing sugars, such as glucose, in a food sample?
a: Benedict's test detects reducing sugars: a blue Benedict's solution turns green, then yellow, then brick-red/orange precipitate when heated with a reducing sugar present.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: An enzyme is best described as:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** a biological catalyst that speeds up chemical reactions without being used up

Enzymes are biological catalysts, usually proteins, that speed up specific biochemical reactions without being permanently changed or used up themselves.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: According to the lock-and-key model, an enzyme is specific to its substrate because:
a: The lock-and-key model explains enzyme specificity: only a substrate with a shape that fits the enzyme's active site can bind and react.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Most human enzymes work best at an optimum temperature of approximately:
a: Most human enzymes have an optimum temperature around 37 degrees Celsius, matching normal human body temperature.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: At temperatures well above an enzyme's optimum, its activity decreases mainly because:
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** the enzyme's active site becomes denatured and changes shape

High temperatures cause the enzyme's protein structure, including the active site, to denature (change shape irreversibly), so it can no longer bind its substrate effectively.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The overall word equation for photosynthesis is:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** carbon dioxide + water --(light energy)--> glucose + oxygen

Photosynthesis combines carbon dioxide and water, using light energy trapped by chlorophyll, to produce glucose and oxygen.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis is called:
a: Chlorophyll is the green pigment found in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy, mainly in the red and blue parts of the spectrum, to drive photosynthesis.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which of the following is NOT a limiting factor of photosynthesis?
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** Soil pH only

The main limiting factors of photosynthesis are light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature; soil pH alone is not considered a primary limiting factor of the photosynthesis reaction itself.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Stomata on a leaf mainly function to allow:
a: Stomata are small pores, mainly on the underside of leaves, that allow gaseous exchange (carbon dioxide entering for photosynthesis, oxygen and water vapour leaving) and are controlled by guard cells.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A mineral deficiency causing yellowing of leaves (chlorosis) due to lack of chlorophyll production is most associated with a lack of:
a: Magnesium is a key component of the chlorophyll molecule; a deficiency causes yellowing of leaves (chlorosis) as less chlorophyll can be made.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A deficiency of nitrate ions in a plant typically causes:
a: Nitrate is needed to make amino acids and proteins for growth; a deficiency causes stunted growth and yellowing (chlorosis), particularly of older leaves.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A balanced diet should contain all of the following EXCEPT:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** only water, with no other nutrients

A balanced diet requires carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water together, not water alone.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which vitamin deficiency is most closely associated with the disease scurvy?
a: A deficiency of vitamin C causes scurvy, characterised by bleeding gums and poor wound healing, since vitamin C is needed for healthy connective tissue.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which enzyme, found in saliva, begins the digestion of starch in the mouth?
a: Salivary amylase breaks down starch into maltose, beginning carbohydrate digestion in the mouth.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Pepsin is an enzyme that digests proteins and works best in the:
a: Pepsin is secreted in the stomach and works optimally in the strongly acidic conditions created by hydrochloric acid there.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Bile, produced by the liver, aids digestion mainly by:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** emulsifying fats into smaller droplets to increase surface area for lipase

Bile emulsifies large fat droplets into smaller ones, increasing the surface area available for lipase enzymes to break down fats more efficiently. Bile itself is not an enzyme.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The main site of absorption of digested food into the bloodstream is the:
a: The small intestine, with its highly folded lining covered in villi, is the main site where digested nutrients are absorbed into the blood.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Villi in the small intestine increase the efficiency of absorption mainly by:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** increasing the surface area available for absorption

Villi are finger-like projections that greatly increase the surface area of the small intestine lining, maximising nutrient absorption into the blood.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The main function of the large intestine is to:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** absorb water from undigested food, forming faeces

The large intestine mainly absorbs water (and some salts) from the remaining undigested material, forming and compacting faeces.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Peristalsis refers to:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** wave-like muscular contractions that push food along the gut

Peristalsis is the rhythmic, wave-like contraction of muscles in the wall of the alimentary canal that pushes food along its length.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which of the following food tests would turn purple/lilac in the presence of protein?
a: The Biuret test detects protein: sodium hydroxide and dilute copper sulphate turn from blue to purple/lilac in the presence of protein.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Water and mineral ions are transported upward through a plant mainly in the:
a: Xylem tissue transports water and dissolved mineral ions from the roots upward through the plant to the leaves.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Manufactured food (sugars), mainly sucrose, is transported around a plant in the:
a: Phloem tissue transports the products of photosynthesis (mainly sucrose), a process called translocation, from the leaves to other parts of the plant.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Transpiration is best defined as:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through stomata

Transpiration is the evaporation and loss of water vapour from a plant's surface, mainly through the stomata of the leaves.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which of the following conditions would generally INCREASE the rate of transpiration?
a: Increased wind speed removes water vapour from around the leaf surface quickly, maintaining a steep diffusion gradient and increasing the rate of transpiration.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The continuous column of water moving through a plant from roots to leaves, pulled by transpiration, is known as the:
a: The transpiration stream is the continuous movement of water from the roots, through the xylem, to the leaves, driven largely by water loss (transpiration) from the leaves.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Guard cells control the opening and closing of stomata mainly by changes in their:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** turgidity

Guard cells change shape as they become turgid (swollen with water) or flaccid, opening or closing the stomatal pore between them.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A plant wilts mainly because:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** cells lose turgidity as water loss exceeds water uptake

Wilting occurs when transpiration (water loss) exceeds water uptake by the roots, so cells lose turgor pressure and the plant droops.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The chamber of the human heart that pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body is the:
a: The left ventricle has the thickest muscular wall and pumps oxygenated blood at high pressure to the whole body via the aorta.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart, usually under high pressure, are called:
a: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, generally under high pressure, and have thick, muscular, elastic walls.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Capillaries are adapted for efficient exchange of substances with tissues mainly because they have:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** walls one cell thick, providing a short diffusion distance

Capillary walls are only one cell thick, providing a very short diffusion distance for oxygen, nutrients and waste to exchange between blood and body tissues.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which blood component is mainly responsible for transporting oxygen around the body?
a: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds to oxygen in the lungs and releases it to body tissues.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Platelets in the blood are mainly responsible for:
a: Platelets are cell fragments involved in the blood clotting process, helping to seal wounds and prevent excessive blood loss.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Veins differ from arteries in that veins:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** have valves to prevent backflow of blood

Veins carry blood back to the heart under lower pressure and contain valves to prevent the backflow of blood, especially in the limbs.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The double circulatory system in humans means that blood passes through the heart:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** twice for each complete circuit of the body (once to the lungs, once to the body)

In a double circulatory system, blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit: once via pulmonary circulation to the lungs and once via systemic circulation to the rest of the body.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Pathogens are best described as:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** organisms that cause disease

Pathogens are disease-causing organisms or agents, such as bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Cholera is a disease caused mainly by:
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** a bacterium spread through contaminated water

Cholera is caused by a bacterium and is typically spread through water or food contaminated with the faeces of an infected person.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Malaria is transmitted to humans mainly through:
a: Malaria is caused by a Plasmodium parasite transmitted through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Bilharzia (schistosomiasis) is contracted mainly by:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** contact with water containing infected freshwater snails releasing larvae

Bilharzia is caused by parasitic flatworms whose larvae are released by infected freshwater snails and can penetrate human skin during contact with contaminated water.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: White blood cells that engulf and digest pathogens by phagocytosis are called:
a: Phagocytes are white blood cells that engulf and digest pathogens through a process called phagocytosis.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Lymphocytes provide immunity mainly by:
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** producing antibodies specific to particular antigens

Lymphocytes are white blood cells that produce antibodies specific to particular antigens found on pathogens, helping to neutralise or mark them for destruction.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Vaccination provides immunity by:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** introducing a weakened or inactive form of a pathogen so the body produces antibodies and memory cells

Vaccines contain a weakened, inactive, or partial form of a pathogen that stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells, providing future protection.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) primarily attacks which type of cell in the body?
a: HIV attacks and destroys T-helper lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell important for coordinating the immune response, progressively weakening the body's immunity.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which of the following is a correct method for preventing the spread of cholera in a community?
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** Ensuring safe water supply and proper sanitation/sewage disposal

Since cholera spreads through water or food contaminated with faecal matter, ensuring safe drinking water and proper sanitation are the most effective preventive measures.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The tiny air sacs in the lungs where gaseous exchange occurs are called:
a: Alveoli are tiny, thin-walled air sacs surrounded by capillaries, where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged between the air and the blood.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Alveoli are adapted for efficient gaseous exchange mainly because they have:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** a large surface area, thin walls, and a good blood supply

Alveoli have a large total surface area, very thin (one-cell-thick) walls, and a rich capillary blood supply, all maximising the rate of gaseous exchange by diffusion.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: During inhalation, the diaphragm:
a: During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens, increasing the volume of the chest cavity, which draws air into the lungs.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which structure prevents food from entering the trachea during swallowing?
a: The epiglottis is a flap of tissue that closes over the entrance to the trachea (windpipe) during swallowing, directing food into the oesophagus instead.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Cilia and mucus in the trachea and bronchi mainly function to:
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** trap and remove dust, pathogens and debris from the airways

Mucus traps dust, debris and pathogens in inhaled air, while cilia sweep this mucus upward toward the throat to be swallowed or expelled, keeping airways clear.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which of the following correctly compares inhaled and exhaled air?
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** Exhaled air contains less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than inhaled air

During gaseous exchange, oxygen is absorbed into the blood and carbon dioxide is released, so exhaled air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than inhaled air.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Smoking damages the lungs partly because tar and chemicals in cigarette smoke:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** destroy cilia and can cause chronic bronchitis and lung cancer

Chemicals in cigarette smoke damage and destroy cilia (reducing the lungs' ability to clear mucus and debris) and can cause chronic bronchitis, emphysema and lung cancer over time.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The word equation for aerobic respiration is:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water (+ energy)

Aerobic respiration breaks down glucose using oxygen to release energy, producing carbon dioxide and water as by-products.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells (during vigorous exercise) produces:
a: In human muscle cells, anaerobic respiration (in the absence of enough oxygen) breaks down glucose incompletely to produce lactic acid, releasing less energy than aerobic respiration.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** ethanol and carbon dioxide

Anaerobic respiration in yeast (fermentation) breaks down glucose to produce ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Compared to aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration releases:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** much less energy per glucose molecule

Anaerobic respiration releases far less energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration, since glucose is only partially broken down.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: 'Oxygen debt' refers to the:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down accumulated lactic acid

Oxygen debt is the extra oxygen the body needs after strenuous exercise to break down the lactic acid that built up during anaerobic respiration.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Excretion is best defined as:
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** the removal of metabolic waste products made by the body's own cells

Excretion is the removal from the body of waste products of metabolism (such as carbon dioxide and urea), which is different from egestion (removal of undigested food waste/faeces).
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The main organ responsible for filtering blood and producing urine is the:
a: The kidneys filter the blood, removing urea and excess substances, and produce urine as a result.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Urea is produced mainly in the:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** liver, by the breakdown of excess amino acids (deamination)

The liver breaks down excess amino acids in a process called deamination, producing urea, which is then transported to the kidneys for removal from the blood.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The functional unit of the kidney, responsible for filtration and reabsorption, is called the:
a: The nephron is the microscopic functional unit of the kidney where blood filtration and selective reabsorption take place.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Homeostasis is best defined as:
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** the maintenance of a constant internal environment within the body

Homeostasis is the regulation of the internal environment of the body (e.g. temperature, water balance, blood glucose) to maintain relatively stable, constant conditions.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: When body temperature rises above normal, sweating helps cool the body mainly through:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** evaporation of sweat from the skin surface, removing heat energy

Sweat evaporates from the skin surface, and this evaporation requires heat energy taken from the skin, cooling the body down.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: When the body is cold, blood vessels near the skin surface narrow in a process called:
a: Vasoconstriction is the narrowing of blood vessels near the skin surface, reducing blood flow to the skin and therefore reducing heat loss when the body is cold.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Shivering helps to warm the body because:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** rapid muscle contractions release heat energy through increased respiration

Shivering involves rapid, involuntary muscle contractions, which increase the rate of respiration in muscle cells, releasing heat as a by-product and warming the body.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The hormone insulin, produced by the pancreas, helps regulate blood glucose by:
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** causing cells to absorb glucose and the liver to convert glucose to glycogen, lowering blood glucose

Insulin lowers blood glucose levels by stimulating cells to take up glucose and the liver to convert excess glucose into glycogen for storage.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Diabetes mellitus (Type 1) is caused mainly by:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** insufficient production of insulin by the pancreas

Type 1 diabetes results from the pancreas producing insufficient (or no) insulin, leading to poorly controlled, often elevated, blood glucose levels.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The human skeleton provides all of the following functions EXCEPT:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** production of digestive enzymes

The skeleton provides support, protection, movement (via muscle attachment), and blood cell production (in bone marrow), but does not produce digestive enzymes.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A joint where bones meet and movement occurs is held together by tough connective tissue called:
a: Ligaments are tough, elastic connective tissue that join bone to bone at a joint, providing stability while allowing movement.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Tendons connect:
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** muscle to bone

Tendons are tough connective tissue that attach muscles to bones, allowing muscle contraction to move the skeleton.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: At the elbow joint, the biceps and triceps muscles work as an antagonistic pair, meaning:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** as one contracts, the other relaxes, producing opposite movements

Antagonistic muscle pairs work in opposition: as the biceps contracts to bend the arm, the triceps relaxes, and vice versa when straightening the arm.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Cartilage found at the ends of bones in a joint mainly functions to:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** reduce friction and absorb shock between bones

Cartilage covers the ends of bones at a joint, providing a smooth surface that reduces friction and absorbs shock during movement.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A ball-and-socket joint, such as the hip joint, allows movement in:
a: Ball-and-socket joints, such as the hip and shoulder, allow a wide range of movement in multiple directions, including rotation.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Bone marrow found inside certain bones is important because it:
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** produces red and white blood cells

Bone marrow, found within certain bones, is the site of production of red blood cells and some white blood cells.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The basic functional unit of the nervous system is the:
a: A neuron (nerve cell) is the basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system, transmitting electrical impulses.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A reflex action is best described as:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** a rapid, automatic and involuntary response to a stimulus

A reflex action is a fast, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus that does not require conscious thought, such as withdrawing a hand from a hot surface.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The correct order of a simple reflex arc is:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** receptor -> sensory neuron -> relay neuron (spinal cord) -> motor neuron -> effector

A reflex arc passes from a receptor, along a sensory neuron, through a relay neuron in the spinal cord, along a motor neuron, to an effector (muscle or gland), producing a rapid response.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The part of the eye that controls the amount of light entering the eye by changing the size of the pupil is the:
a: The iris is a ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil, regulating the amount of light entering the eye.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Light-sensitive cells that detect light and form images are found in the:
a: The retina contains light-sensitive receptor cells (rods and cones) that detect light and send nerve impulses to the brain via the optic nerve.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The gap between two neurons, across which a nerve impulse is transmitted chemically, is called a:
a: A synapse is the small gap between two neurons where the nerve impulse is transmitted from one neuron to the next using chemical neurotransmitters.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The central nervous system in humans consists of the:
a: The central nervous system (CNS) is made up of the brain and spinal cord, which process and coordinate information from throughout the body.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which part of the brain is mainly responsible for controlling balance and coordination of movement?
a: The cerebellum is mainly responsible for coordinating fine movement, posture and balance.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Hormones are transported around the body in the:
a: Hormones are chemical messengers secreted by endocrine glands directly into the blood, which carries them to target organs around the body.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Compared to nervous responses, hormonal responses are generally:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** slower and longer-lasting

Hormonal (endocrine) responses are generally slower to take effect but longer-lasting compared to fast, short-lived nervous responses.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Adrenaline, released by the adrenal glands, prepares the body for 'fight or flight' by:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** increasing heart rate, breathing rate and blood glucose levels

Adrenaline increases heart rate, breathing rate and blood glucose levels, preparing the body for rapid physical action in response to stress or danger.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The gland often called the 'master gland' because it controls many other endocrine glands is the:
a: The pituitary gland, located at the base of the brain, is called the 'master gland' because it produces hormones that regulate the activity of many other endocrine glands.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The thyroid gland produces a hormone that mainly controls:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** the body's metabolic rate

The thyroid gland produces thyroxine, a hormone that regulates the body's basal metabolic rate, affecting growth and energy use.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which of the following is an example of a negative feedback mechanism in the body?
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** Insulin lowering blood glucose when it rises, and glucagon raising it when it falls too low

Negative feedback mechanisms detect a change from the normal set point and trigger a response that reverses that change, such as insulin/glucagon regulating blood glucose to keep it within a stable range.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A drug that slows down the activity of the nervous system, such as alcohol, is classified as a:
a: Depressants, such as alcohol, slow down the activity of the central nervous system, reducing brain and body function.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A drug that increases the activity of the nervous system, such as caffeine, is classified as a:
a: Stimulants, such as caffeine and nicotine, increase the activity of the nervous system, making a person feel more alert.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Drug addiction is best described as:
a: Addiction involves a physical and/or psychological dependence on a drug, often producing withdrawal symptoms (such as cravings, anxiety or physical discomfort) when use is stopped.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Long-term heavy alcohol consumption is most strongly associated with damage to the:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** liver (e.g. cirrhosis)

Long-term heavy alcohol use is strongly associated with liver damage, including cirrhosis, since the liver breaks down alcohol and can become scarred from prolonged exposure.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Antibiotics are used to treat infections caused by:
a: Antibiotics work against bacteria by killing them or stopping their growth; they are not effective against viruses.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which of the following best explains why antibiotic misuse (e.g. not completing a full course) is a public health concern?
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** It can lead to antibiotic-resistant bacteria developing

Incomplete or inappropriate antibiotic use allows surviving bacteria (which may have some resistance) to multiply, contributing to the development of antibiotic-resistant strains.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: In human males, sperm cells are produced in the:
a: Sperm cells are produced in the testes through the process of meiosis.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: In human females, egg cells (ova) mature and are released from the:
a: Egg cells mature within follicles in the ovary, and one is typically released (ovulation) around the middle of each menstrual cycle.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Fertilisation in humans normally occurs in the:
a: Fertilisation, the fusion of a sperm and egg cell, normally takes place in the oviduct (fallopian tube).
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The placenta functions mainly to:
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** allow exchange of nutrients, oxygen and waste between mother and foetus

The placenta is the organ that allows the exchange of nutrients, oxygen, and waste products between the mother's blood and the developing foetus's blood, without the two blood supplies mixing directly.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: During the menstrual cycle, the lining of the uterus (endometrium) breaks down and is shed if:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** fertilisation has NOT occurred

If the released egg is not fertilised, hormone levels fall, causing the thickened uterus lining to break down and be shed as menstruation.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which method of contraception works by creating a physical barrier preventing sperm from reaching an egg?
a: A condom is a barrier method of contraception that physically prevents sperm from reaching and fertilising an egg.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: In flowering plants, pollination is best defined as:
a: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther (male part) to the stigma (female part) of a flower, which may be of the same or a different flower.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A seed requires which of the following conditions to germinate?
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** Water, oxygen and a suitable temperature

Seeds generally require sufficient water, oxygen for respiration, and a suitable (usually warm) temperature to germinate successfully.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The chromosome number in a normal human body (somatic) cell is:
a: Normal human body (somatic) cells contain 46 chromosomes, arranged in 23 homologous pairs.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Human sex cells (gametes) contain how many chromosomes?
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** 23, half the number found in body cells

Gametes (sperm and egg cells) contain 23 chromosomes, half the number in normal body cells, produced through meiosis, so that fertilisation restores the full 46.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: In humans, the sex of a baby is determined by which chromosomes it inherits, specifically:
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** XX for female, XY for male

In humans, females have two X chromosomes (XX) and males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY); the father's sperm determines the baby's sex depending on whether it carries an X or Y chromosome.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A gene is best defined as:
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** a section of DNA that codes for a particular characteristic/protein

A gene is a specific section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a particular protein, which in turn influences a particular characteristic.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: If both parents are heterozygous for a recessive genetic condition (Aa x Aa), what proportion of their offspring is expected to show the recessive condition?
a: A cross between two heterozygous parents (Aa x Aa) produces offspring in the ratio 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, meaning 25% (1 in 4) are expected to be homozygous recessive (aa) and show the recessive condition.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: An allele that is expressed in the phenotype even when only one copy is present (in a heterozygous individual) is called:
a: A dominant allele is expressed in the phenotype whenever it is present, even alongside a different (recessive) allele in a heterozygous individual.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Sickle cell anaemia is an example of a genetic condition inherited as a:
a: Sickle cell anaemia is inherited as a recessive allele; a person needs two copies of the sickle cell allele (homozygous recessive) to have the full condition.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Variation between offspring of the same two parents mainly arises from:
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** meiosis (crossing over and independent assortment) and random fertilisation

Genetic variation among offspring arises mainly from processes during meiosis (such as crossing over and independent assortment of chromosomes) and the random combination of gametes at fertilisation.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Continuous variation (e.g. human height) differs from discontinuous variation (e.g. human blood group) mainly because continuous variation:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** shows a range of values with many intermediates, often influenced by both genes and environment

Continuous variation produces a full range of values with intermediates (e.g. height), usually influenced by multiple genes and environmental factors, unlike discontinuous variation which falls into distinct categories.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Natural selection is best described as the process by which:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** organisms with advantageous characteristics are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing on those characteristics

Natural selection is the process where individuals with characteristics better suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing those advantageous characteristics to offspring over generations.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is an example of:
a: When antibiotics are used, susceptible bacteria die while any naturally resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, illustrating natural selection favouring resistance over generations.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Selective breeding (artificial selection) differs from natural selection mainly because in selective breeding:
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** humans choose which organisms with desired traits are bred together

In selective breeding, humans (not natural environmental pressures) deliberately choose organisms with desirable characteristics to breed, gradually increasing the frequency of those traits.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: A species is generally defined as a group of organisms that can:
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** interbreed and produce fertile offspring

A species is generally defined as a group of organisms capable of interbreeding with one another to produce fertile offspring.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Adaptation refers to:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** a feature that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment

An adaptation is an inherited feature that increases an organism's chances of survival and successful reproduction in its particular environment.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: In a food chain, the arrow between organisms represents:
a: In a food chain, the arrow shows the direction of energy transfer, pointing from the organism being eaten to the organism that eats it.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Organisms that make their own food using light energy, forming the base of most food chains, are called:
a: Producers, mainly green plants and algae, make their own food through photosynthesis and form the base of almost all food chains.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Organisms that break down dead organic matter and waste, recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem, are called:
a: Decomposers, such as certain bacteria and fungi, break down dead organisms and waste material, releasing nutrients back into the ecosystem.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Only about 10% of energy is typically transferred from one trophic level to the next in a food chain, mainly because energy is lost through:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** respiration, movement, heat loss and undigested/egested material

Energy is lost at each trophic level mainly through respiration (as heat), movement, and material that is not eaten, digested or absorbed, meaning only a small proportion is passed to the next level.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Deforestation can lead to which of the following environmental problems?
a: Deforestation removes tree roots that hold soil in place and provide habitat, leading to increased soil erosion, habitat loss, and reduced biodiversity.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: The excessive use of chemical fertilisers running off into rivers and lakes can cause a problem known as:
a: Eutrophication occurs when excess nutrients (such as from fertiliser run-off) enter water bodies, causing algal blooms that block light and, when they decompose, deplete oxygen and kill aquatic life.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Conservation of wildlife and natural habitats is important mainly because it:
a: Conservation maintains biodiversity and ecological balance, protects resources (such as clean water and fertile soil), and preserves natural heritage for future generations.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: An ecosystem is best defined as:
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** a community of living organisms interacting with each other and their non-living environment

An ecosystem includes both a community of interacting living organisms (biotic factors) and the non-living physical environment (abiotic factors) they interact with.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which of the following is an abiotic (non-living) factor that can affect the population size of organisms in an ecosystem?
a: Temperature and rainfall are abiotic (non-living, physical) factors that can significantly affect population size, unlike predation, competition and disease, which are biotic factors.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice Practice

q: Which characteristic of living organisms refers to the process of taking in and using food for energy and growth?
a: Nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain and use food to provide energy and materials for growth and repair.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: In binomial nomenclature, the first part of an organism's scientific name represents its:
a: In binomial nomenclature, the first word (capitalised) is the genus, and the second word (lowercase) is the species, e.g. Panthera leo.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Name one single-celled eukaryotic organism classified in the kingdom Protoctista and state two of its features.
a: Amoeba is a single-celled organism with a nucleus, classified in the kingdom Protoctista, distinct from bacteria, fungi and plants.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Insects, spiders and crustaceans are all classified under the phylum:
a: Arthropods are characterised by a hard exoskeleton, segmented body and jointed limbs, and include insects, arachnids (e.g. spiders) and crustaceans.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Vertebrates are animals that have:
a: Vertebrates are animals possessing a backbone (vertebral column) as part of an internal skeleton, e.g. fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Which feature is used to distinguish mammals from other vertebrate classes?
a: Mammals are distinguished by having mammary glands that produce milk to feed their young, and (in almost all cases) hair or fur.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Name the kingdom to which yeast belongs and state two features that distinguish it from plants.
a: Yeast is a single-celled fungus, correctly classified under Kingdom Fungi.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Which structure is responsible for protein synthesis within a cell?
a: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis within a cell, translating genetic information into proteins.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Name two cell structures found in both plant and animal cells and state the function of one of them.
a: Mitochondria are found in both plant and animal cells, since both carry out aerobic respiration; cell walls, chloroplasts and large permanent vacuoles are typically only found in plant cells.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: The cell membrane is described as 'partially permeable' because it:
a: A partially (selectively) permeable membrane allows some substances to pass through while restricting others, based on factors such as size and solubility.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: State the main function of the cytoplasm within a living cell.
a: Cytoplasm is the jelly-like substance filling the cell, in which organelles are suspended and many metabolic reactions occur.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Ciliated epithelial cells lining the trachea are specialised by having:
a: Ciliated cells have tiny hair-like cilia on their surface that beat rhythmically to sweep mucus (with trapped dust and pathogens) away from the lungs.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Sperm cells are specially adapted for their function by having:
a: Sperm cells have a tail (flagellum) that enables swimming movement, and many mitochondria packed in the mid-piece to provide energy for this movement.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: When placed in a solution with the same water potential as its own cytoplasm (isotonic), a plant cell will:
a: In an isotonic solution, there is no overall difference in water potential, so there is no net movement of water into or out of the cell, and its size stays roughly the same.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: State three factors that increase the rate of diffusion of a gas across a biological membrane.
a: Increasing the surface area available for diffusion increases the rate at which particles can move across a membrane; a steeper concentration gradient, thinner membrane, and higher temperature would also increase diffusion rate.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Why is active transport important for root hair cells absorbing certain mineral ions from soil?
a: Since mineral ion concentration is often higher inside root hair cells than in the surrounding soil, active transport (using energy) is required to move ions against this concentration gradient.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: A named example of a tissue in the human body, made up of similar cells performing one function, is:
a: Muscle tissue is made up of many similar muscle cells working together to contract and produce movement, making it a correct example of a tissue.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: An organ system is best described as:
a: An organ system consists of multiple organs working together to carry out a major body function, such as the digestive system (mouth, oesophagus, stomach, intestines, etc.) working together to digest food.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Which level of biological organisation comes directly between 'cell' and 'organ' in order of increasing complexity?
a: The correct order of biological organisation is: cell -> tissue -> organ -> organ system -> organism, so tissue falls directly between cell and organ.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Guard cells surrounding a stoma are unusual among epidermal cells because they contain:
a: Unlike most other epidermal cells, guard cells contain chloroplasts, which contribute to changes in turgor pressure that open and close the stomatal pore.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: A student places pieces of potato in three different sugar solutions and measures their mass before and after. This investigation is most likely designed to study:
a: Measuring mass change in plant tissue placed in solutions of differing concentration is a classic practical method for investigating osmosis and water movement.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: White blood cells are able to change shape and engulf pathogens partly because they lack:
a: Like other animal cells, white blood cells lack a rigid cell wall, allowing them flexibility to change shape and engulf pathogens by phagocytosis.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Which statement correctly compares a light microscope with an electron microscope?
a: Electron microscopes use beams of electrons rather than light, achieving much higher magnification and resolution than light microscopes, revealing fine internal detail of organelles.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Carbohydrates are made up of the elements:
a: Carbohydrates contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, typically in a ratio where hydrogen and oxygen occur in a 2:1 ratio as in water.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Glycogen in animals and starch in plants both serve mainly as:
a: Glycogen (in animals) and starch (in plants) are both storage carbohydrates made of many linked glucose units, providing an energy reserve.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Fats and oils are made up of one molecule of glycerol combined with:
a: A fat (lipid) molecule consists of one glycerol molecule bonded to three fatty acid molecules.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: When testing a food sample for fats, the ethanol emulsion test gives a positive result shown by:
a: In the ethanol emulsion test, fat dissolves in ethanol and then forms a cloudy white emulsion when the mixture is added to water, indicating the presence of fat.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Enzyme activity graphs typically show that as substrate concentration increases (with enzyme concentration fixed), the rate of reaction:
a: As substrate concentration increases, reaction rate increases until all available enzyme active sites are occupied (saturated), after which adding more substrate has no further effect on rate.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: A change in pH away from an enzyme's optimum can reduce its activity mainly because it:
a: A pH away from the optimum can disrupt the bonds maintaining an enzyme's shape, altering the active site and reducing its ability to bind its substrate.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Pepsin, an enzyme produced in the stomach, would become far less effective if the stomach's pH became:
a: Pepsin's optimum working environment is strongly acidic; a shift to alkaline conditions would denature or reduce the effectiveness of the enzyme.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: An investigation shows amylase breaking down starch fastest at 37 degrees Celsius, with activity falling off sharply above 45 degrees Celsius. This fall in activity above 45 degrees Celsius is best explained by:
a: At temperatures well above the optimum, enzymes denature: their protein structure, including the active site, is permanently altered, sharply reducing activity.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: In an investigation of photosynthesis using pondweed, the number of oxygen bubbles produced per minute is often used to measure:
a: Since oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, counting bubbles produced by pondweed per minute is a common way to estimate the rate of photosynthesis under different conditions.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: A leaf that has been destarched (starch removed) and then partly covered with foil and exposed to light is later tested with iodine. The uncovered part turns blue-black while the covered part does not. This shows that:
a: Only the part exposed to light turned blue-black (indicating starch), showing that light is necessary for photosynthesis (and therefore starch production) to occur.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Increasing carbon dioxide concentration around a plant will increase the rate of photosynthesis only up to a point, after which:
a: Once carbon dioxide is no longer the limiting factor, another factor (such as light intensity or temperature) will limit further increases in the rate of photosynthesis.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: A farmer notices purple discolouration on the leaves of maize plants. This is most likely a sign of deficiency in which mineral?
a: Phosphate deficiency in plants is commonly associated with poor root growth and purple discolouration of leaves.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: A balanced human diet requires fibre (roughage) mainly to:
a: Fibre is not digested but adds bulk to food, stimulating peristalsis and helping to prevent constipation, supporting healthy bowel movement.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: A diet lacking sufficient protein over a long period, especially in children, can lead to a condition called:
a: Kwashiorkor is caused by severe protein deficiency, commonly resulting in a swollen abdomen and other symptoms, particularly in young children.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Vitamin D deficiency in children is most closely associated with which condition?
a: Vitamin D is required for calcium absorption and bone development; a deficiency in children causes rickets, characterised by soft, weak, deformed bones.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: The correct order of parts of the human alimentary canal, from start to end, is:
a: Food passes in order through the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and finally the rectum/anus.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Trypsin is a protein-digesting enzyme secreted by the:
a: Trypsin is a protein-digesting enzyme produced by the pancreas and released into the small intestine, where it works in the alkaline environment there.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Lipase enzymes digest fats into:
a: Lipase enzymes break down fats (lipids) into fatty acids and glycerol.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Which structure produces hydrochloric acid that kills many bacteria present in swallowed food?
a: Glands in the stomach lining secrete hydrochloric acid, which creates strongly acidic conditions that help kill many bacteria present in food and activate pepsin.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: A person with a diet lacking sufficient iron is at greatest risk of developing:
a: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin; a deficiency leads to anaemia, causing tiredness and pale skin due to reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Explain why food must be mechanically broken down (chewed) before chemical digestion occurs.
a: Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces, increasing the surface area available for digestive enzymes to act on, speeding up chemical digestion.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: A patient whose gall bladder has been removed may have more difficulty digesting which nutrient?
a: The gall bladder stores bile, which emulsifies fats; without stored bile readily available, fat digestion can become less efficient.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Distinguish clearly between digestion and absorption in the human alimentary canal.
a: Digestion is the mechanical and chemical breakdown of food into smaller molecules, while absorption is the separate process of those digested molecules moving into the bloodstream.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: Define the term egestion and explain how it differs from excretion.
a: Egestion is the removal of undigested food waste (faeces) from the body through the anus, distinct from excretion of metabolic waste.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice

q: A potometer is a piece of apparatus commonly used to measure the rate of:
a: A potometer measures the rate of water uptake by a cut shoot, which is used as an estimate of the rate of transpiration.
p: Biology O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory Practice
