a: Hold the convex lens between a distant sunlit object (window/trees) and a white paper screen [1]. Move the screen back and forth until a sharp inverted image appears on the screen [2]. Measure the perpendicular distance from lens centre to screen with a ruler — this equals focal length f [1].
p: Combined Science O-Level Paper 3 — Practical Theory

q: Practical Investigation: Explain how to investigate the extension of a helical spring under increasing slotted masses up to 500 g and plot results safely. [5 marks]
a: Clamp spring vertically beside a metre rule with pointer attached [1]. Record initial pointer reading L₀ with 0 N load [1]. Add 1 N (100 g) weights stepwise up to 5 N, recording new lengths and computing extension e = L - L₀ [2]. Wear eye protection against snapping and plot Load vs Extension to verify proportionality [1].
p: Combined Science O-Level Paper 3 — Practical Theory

q: Practical Investigation: State the positive chemical tests and expected observations for (a) oxygen gas [2 marks], (b) hydrogen gas [2 marks], and (c) ammonia gas [2 marks].
a: (a) Oxygen relights a glowing wooden splint [2 marks]. (b) Hydrogen burns with a squeaky "pop" when a lighted splint is applied [2 marks]. (c) Ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue (pungent smell) [2 marks].
p: Combined Science O-Level Paper 3 — Practical Theory

q:
Practical Investigation: A student conducts paper chromatography on black ink using water as solvent.
(a) Why must the baseline be drawn in pencil rather than ink? [2 marks]
(b) Why must the solvent level start below the ink spot? [1 mark]
a:
(a) Pencil graphite is insoluble in water so it will not dissolve and smear up the chromatogram; ink would run [2 marks].
(b) So the ink spot separates upward by capillary action rather than dissolving straight down into the solvent beaker [1 mark].
p: Combined Science O-Level Paper 3 — Practical Theory

q: Practical Investigation: Describe how to use a ray box, plane mirror, protractor, and white paper to verify the law of reflection. [4 marks]
a: Draw mirror line and perpendicular normal on paper [1]. Shine a narrow incident ray at angle i (e.g. 30°) to the normal and trace both incident and reflected rays with pencil dots [2]. Measure reflected angle r with protractor and repeat for angles 20°–60°, confirming angle i = angle r [1].
p: Combined Science O-Level Paper 3 — Practical Theory

q: Practical Investigation: Describe how to observe onion epidermal cells stained with iodine under a light microscope, explaining why iodine stain is added. [4 marks]
a: Peel a thin transparent inner onion epidermis layer, place flat in a drop of water on a glass slide, add 1 drop of iodine solution, and lower a coverslip gently at an angle to avoid air bubbles [3 marks]. Iodine stains cell nuclei and cell walls brown/yellow so organelles stand out clearly under the microscope [1 mark].
p: Combined Science O-Level Paper 3 — Practical Theory

q: What is commerce?

q: What is home trade?

q: Who buys in bulk from producers and sells to retailers?

q: Who sells mainly to final consumers?

q: Which aid to trade moves goods from one place to another?

q: Which insurance principle requires disclosure of material facts?

q: What is advertising?

q: What is a consumer?
a: The correct answer is A person who uses goods or services. Topic: stock.

q: Why is stock control important?
a: The correct answer is To maintain appropriate stock levels and reduce losses. Topic: pricing.
p: Commerce O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: What is entrepreneurship?

q: What is profit?
a: The correct answer is Revenue minus costs. Topic: SMEs.

q: Which type of warehouse stores imported dutiable goods until customs duty is paid?
a: Bonded warehouses are supervised by ZIMRA until import duties are settled.

q: In foreign trade, what does the Incoterm CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight) mean?
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** Seller's quoted price covers goods cost, marine insurance, and freight to destination port

CIF includes cost of goods, insurance, and sea freight to the named destination port.

q: Which insurance principle prevents an insured person from making a profit out of a partial loss claim?
a: Indemnity restores the insured to the exact financial position before loss—no profit.
p: Commerce O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Which document is issued by a shipowner acknowledging receipt of goods loaded onto a vessel for export?
a: A Bill of Lading serves as receipt, contract of carriage, and document of title to shipped goods.
p: Commerce O-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q:
**Passage:**
Every morning before sunrise, Nyasha walked three kilometres along the dusty footpath to Nyanga Secondary School, carrying her battered canvas satchel. Despite power cuts at home that forced her to revise by solar lantern, she topped Form 3 in Chemistry and English. Her teacher noticed her quiet persistence and nominated her for the district science Olympiad.

(a) Give two challenges Nyasha faced while preparing for school. [2 marks]
(b) What evidence shows that Nyasha was academically successful? [1 mark]
(c) Explain in your own words the meaning of "quiet persistence". [2 marks]
a:
(a) Walking 3 km every morning before sunrise along a dusty path; studying under frequent home power cuts using a solar lantern [2 marks].
(b) She came first in Form 3 Chemistry and English [1 mark].
(c) Determined, steady hard work carried out calmly without boasting or complaining [2 marks].
p: English Language O-Level Paper 2 — Comprehension & Language

q:
**Passage:**
Smallholder irrigation schemes along the Save Valley have transformed formerly drought-prone villages. By replacing open earthen canals—where up to half the water evaporated or seeped away—with lined drip pipes, farmers now harvest green maize and tomatoes twice a year. Youth cooperatives manage pump maintenance and sell surplus produce directly to Mutare markets.

Summary Task (Max 60 words): Summarise the benefits brought by the new irrigation practices to the Save Valley communities. [10 marks]
a: Key summary points (2 marks each for any 5 clear points, continuous prose within word limit): 1. Villages previously vulnerable to drought are transformed. 2. Lined drip pipes stop water loss from evaporation and seepage. 3. Farmers harvest maize and tomatoes twice annually. 4. Youth cooperatives gain technical skills maintaining pumps. 5. Surplus crops sold in Mutare boost household incomes. [10 marks].
p: English Language O-Level Paper 2 — Comprehension & Language

q: Section A Composition (350–450 words): Write a discursive essay titled: "Social media does more harm than good to O-Level students." Discuss both sides before stating your justified conclusion. [30 marks]
a: Mark Scheme: Balanced arguments FOR harm (screen addiction, sleep loss, cyberbullying, misinformation/distraction from revision) [10]; Arguments AGAINST / benefits (educational videos, peer study groups, quick access to past papers/digital libraries) [10]; Clear personal conclusion, logical paragraph linking, varied vocabulary & accurate grammar [10]. Total: [30 marks].
p: English Language O-Level Paper 2 — Comprehension & Language

q: Section B Guided Writing (Speech): As Senior Prefect, write a speech to be delivered at a Parents' Consultation Day proposing three practical ways parents and teachers can curb substance abuse among teenagers. [20 marks]
a: Mark Scheme: Appropriate speech greeting & audience engagement [3]; Three concrete proposals well developed (e.g., open parent-teen dialogue, random school bag checks & counselling support, funding after-school sports/clubs) [12]; Persuasive rhetorical tone, clear paragraphing & grammatical accuracy [5]. Total: [20 marks].
p: English Language O-Level Paper 2 — Comprehension & Language

q: Section B Guided Writing (Formal Report): Following a fire scare in the school laboratory, write an official report to the Headmaster detailing what happened, the cause, and four safety recommendations. [20 marks]
a: Mark Scheme: Report format (TO, FROM, DATE, SUBJECT) [3]; Objective chronological account & clear root cause (e.g., unattended Bunsen burner near ethanol bottle) [7]; Four actionable recommendations (fire extinguishers serviced, safety briefing, locked chemical store, emergency drill) [6]; Formal impersonal register & accuracy [4]. Total: [20 marks].
p: English Language O-Level Paper 2 — Comprehension & Language

q: Section A Narrative Composition (350–450 words): Write a story ending with the words: "...Looking back at the charred ruins, I realised how costly a single moment of carelessness had been." [30 marks]
a: Mark Scheme: Smooth realistic plot build-up leading credibly to a fire/accident caused by carelessness [14]; Vivid sensory description, suspense, and emotional reflection [8]; Seamless ending with the exact required sentence and clean mechanics [8]. Total: [30 marks].
p: English Language O-Level Paper 2 — Comprehension & Language

q: Section B Formal Letter: You noticed broken streetlights and uncollected refuse along your suburb's main road. Write a letter to the Town Clerk urging council action and proposing community support. [20 marks]
a: Mark Scheme: Two formal addresses, date, Dear Sir/Madam, underlined heading [4]; Clear explanation of safety & health hazards (night crime, disease vectors) + constructive offer of residents' clean-up partnership [11]; Polite firm tone & Yours faithfully close [5]. Total: [20 marks].
p: English Language O-Level Paper 2 — Comprehension & Language

q:
Grammar & Register Editing: Rewrite the following faulty sentences correctly:
(a) "Myself and Tendai we went to Bulawayo yesterday." [2 marks]
(b) "The teacher insisted that everyone must bring their own calculator." (Keep formal concord) [2 marks]
(c) "Being a rainy day, the match was cancelled." (Fix dangling participle) [2 marks]
a:
(a) Tendai and I went to Bulawayo yesterday [2 marks].
(b) The teacher insisted that everyone bring his or her own calculator [2 marks].
(c) Since it was a rainy day, the match was cancelled [2 marks].
p: English Language O-Level Paper 2 — Comprehension & Language

q: Register & Tone Exercise: Explain why the reply "Shut up and wait outside!" is inappropriate when spoken by a hospital receptionist to an elderly patient, and rewrite it politely in appropriate register. [4 marks]
a: It is rude, aggressive, disrespectful toward an elder, and violates professional healthcare empathy/Ubuntu [2 marks]. Polite alternative: "Good morning, Gogo/Sekuru. Kindly take a seat in the waiting area and the nurse will call you shortly." [2 marks].
p: English Language O-Level Paper 2 — Comprehension & Language

q:
Vocabulary in Context: Read: "Although the committee's initial proposal met stiff resistance, the chairperson's tactful compromises gradually placated even the sharpest critics."

a: (a) Strong, determined opposition [2 marks]. (b) Sensitive, diplomatic, avoiding giving unnecessary offence [2 marks]. (c) Calmed down or satisfied angry critics [2 marks].
p: English Language O-Level Paper 2 — Comprehension & Language

q:
Indigenous Religion & Identity:
(a) State four titles/names used for the Supreme Being (Mwari) in Zimbabwean Indigenous Religion. [4 marks]
(b) Explain the importance of totems (mitupo/izibongo) in preserving family unity and nature conservation. [6 marks]
a:
(a) Musikavanhu, Nyadenga, Dzivaguru, Matangakugara, uMvelinqangi / uNkulunkulu [4].
(b) Totems build instant clan hospitality across strangers [2], prohibit incestuous marriage within same-totem clans [2], and deter killing/eating one's totem animal, protecting biodiversity [2].
p: Family and Religious Studies O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Essay

q:
Unhu / Ubuntu & Family Life:
(a) Define the concept of Unhu/Ubuntu. [2 marks]
(b) Discuss four ways extended families support vulnerable children and elderly relatives in Zimbabwe. [8 marks]
a:
(a) African moral philosophy stressing shared humanity, compassion, honesty, and respect ("Munhu munhu nekuda kwevanhu") [2].
(b) Absorbing orphans ("nhaka"/kinship fostering) instead of leaving them homeless [2]; pooling school fees/food in crises [2]; grandparents imparting moral wisdom & folklore [2]; caring physically for sick/elderly parents [2].
p: Family and Religious Studies O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Essay

q:
Christianity in Action:
(a) Outline Jesus' teaching on forgiveness as shown in a named parable (e.g., Unforgiving Servant or Prodigal Son). [4 marks]
(b) Suggest three ways Christian churches in Zimbabwe promote reconciliation after conflict. [6 marks]
a:
(a) In the Prodigal Son (Luke 15), the father welcomes back his repentant wayward son with embrace and celebration rather than vengeance, teaching unlimited mercy [4].
(b) Mediating family/community disputes peacefully; pastoral counselling & forgiveness workshops; preaching national unity and anti-violence [6].
p: Family and Religious Studies O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Essay

q:
Islam — Beliefs & Practices:
(a) List the Five Pillars of Islam in English (or Arabic). [5 marks]
(b) Explain how Zakat and Sawm benefit both the individual believer and wider society. [5 marks]
a:
(a) Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (five daily prayers), Zakat (obligatory almsgiving), Sawm (Ramadan fasting), Hajj (Mecca pilgrimage) [5].
(b) Zakat redistributes wealth to relieve poverty and widows/orphans [2.5]; Sawm cultivates self-control and deepens empathy for the hungry, inspiring generosity [2.5].
p: Family and Religious Studies O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Essay

q:
Judaism:
(a) State four dietary laws/features of Kosher (Kashrut) eating in Judaism. [4 marks]
(b) Explain the religious significance of the Synagogue in Jewish community life. [6 marks]
a:
(a) Pork and shellfish are forbidden; land animals must chew cud and have split hooves; meat and dairy are never cooked/eaten together; slaughter must be humane (Shechita) [4].
(b) Serves as house of prayer (Bet Tefilah), Torah study school (Bet Midrash), and social welfare gathering centre (Bet Knesset) preserving identity [6].
p: Family and Religious Studies O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Essay

q:
Religion & Gender Equality:
(a) Identify three negative cultural or religious practices that have historically disadvantaged women/girls. [3 marks]
(b) Explain how modern religious teachings and Zimbabwean law promote gender equality in leadership and education. [7 marks]
a:
(a) Child pledging/early marriage; unequal inheritance depriving widows; barring women from decision-making roles [3].
(b) Scripture affirms male and female created equally in God's image; Zimbabwe's Constitution criminalises child marriage and guarantees equal property/education access; many churches ordain women pastors and fund girls' STEM/leadership schooling [7].
p: Family and Religious Studies O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Essay

q:
Religion & Environmental Stewardship:
(a) Describe two traditional taboos/customs in Indigenous Religion that protect water sources or forests. [4 marks]
(b) Compare Christian and Islamic teachings on human stewardship of the Earth. [6 marks]
a:
(a) Sacred forests/burial hills (marinda) may not be cut for timber; forbidding soap washing or metal pots at sacred springs protects water purity [4].
(b) Genesis 2:15 tasks humans to "till and keep" creation responsibly; Qur'an appoints humanity as Khalifa (vicegerents/trustees) forbidden from spreading corruption/waste on Earth [6].
p: Family and Religious Studies O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Essay

q:
Religion, Health & Substance Abuse:
(a) State four causes of drug and substance abuse among school-going youth. [4 marks]
(b) Explain how religious values and community programmes can prevent youth substance abuse. [6 marks]
a:
(a) Peer pressure, family breakdown/trauma, idleness/unemployment, cheap illicit availability [4].
(b) Teaching body sanctity and self-discipline; vibrant youth choirs/sports clubs keeping youth constructively engaged; compassionate rehabilitation & peer mentoring without shaming [6].
p: Family and Religious Studies O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Essay

q:
Marriage & Family Responsibilities:
(a) State three causes of marital breakdown in contemporary society. [3 marks]
(b) Discuss four religious values that strengthen stable marriages. [7 marks]
a:
(a) Infidelity, financial secrecy/irresponsibility, domestic violence, poor communication [3].
(b) Unconditional love and mutual respect; marital faithfulness; patient forgiveness; open joint financial planning and prayerful counsel [7].
p: Family and Religious Studies O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Essay

q:
Freedom of Worship & Religious Tolerance:
(a) Explain what religious pluralism means in Zimbabwe. [2 marks]
(b) Give four practical guidelines schools should follow to respect learners of different faiths (ATR, Christianity, Islam, Judaism). [8 marks]
a:
(a) Coexistence of multiple diverse religions within one nation under equal constitutional protection [2].
(b) Respect dietary needs (halal/kosher/pork-free options); avoid mocking minority dress/headscarves; allow reasonable prayer accommodations; teach objective comparative religion fostering empathy [8].
p: Family and Religious Studies O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Essay

q:
Religion & Wealth/Work Ethics:
(a) Explain why hard honest work ("kushanda nesimba") is praised in Indigenous Religion and Christianity. [4 marks]
(b) Contrast ethical wealth creation with exploitation (e.g., underpaying workers or charging extortionate interest). [6 marks]
a:
(a) Proverbs/Pauline teaching condemn laziness ("whoever refuses to work shall not eat"); ATR respects diligent farmers able to host nhimbe and feed orphans [4].
(b) Ethical enterprise creates fair jobs and honours contracts; exploitation harms families and violates scriptural justice ("do not withhold labourers' wages") [6].
p: Family and Religious Studies O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Essay

q:
Death, Bereavement & Afterlife:
(a) Briefly compare beliefs about life after death in Indigenous Religion and Christianity. [6 marks]
(b) State four ways a community shows Unhu during a neighbour's funeral (chema/kuchema). [4 marks]
a:
(a) In ATR, virtuous elders join ancestral spirits (vadzimu) watching over living kin; in Christianity, believers await resurrection and eternal communion with God while rejecting unrepentant sin [6].
(b) Contributing food/chema money; attending night vigil (bira/kuchema) to console bereaved; helping dig/prepare homestead; pausing field work in solidarity [4].
p: Family and Religious Studies O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Essay

q:
Rites of Passage:
(a) Define a "rite of passage" and list three stages of life marked by religious ceremonies. [4 marks]
(b) Describe how naming ceremonies in ATR and infant dedication/baptism in Christianity welcome a new child into community. [6 marks]
a:
(a) A formal ceremony marking transition from one social/spiritual status to another: birth/naming, puberty/initiation, marriage, death [4].
(b) ATR naming connects child to clan ancestors and mutupo heritage; Christian baptism/dedication asks God's blessing and commits parents + congregation to raise the child morally [6].
p: Family and Religious Studies O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Essay

q:
Technology, Media & Morality:
Explain two ways digital media helps religious outreach today, and three moral dangers youths must guard against online. [5 marks]
a: Benefits: Livestreaming sermons to sick/diaspora members; digital sacred texts & study groups [2]. Dangers: Cyberbullying, pornography harming dignity, online gambling/scams, and spreading hate speech/false rumours [3].
p: Family and Religious Studies O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Essay

q:
Conflict Resolution:
Outline a five-step peaceful conflict resolution process informed by religious and Ubuntu principles when two neighbours dispute a boundary fence. [5 marks]
a: 1. Calmly pause hostility and agree to meet with impartial elders/leaders [1]. 2. Allow each side uninterrupted fair hearing [1]. 3. Acknowledge wrongdoing sincerely without pride [1]. 4. Agree a fair restitution/boundary marker [1]. 5. Share goodwill/reconciliation restoring neighbourly harmony [1].
p: Family and Religious Studies O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Essay

q: Explain the role of religious Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs) and faith-based schools/hospitals (e.g., mission hospitals) in Zimbabwe's national development. [6 marks]
a: Build and staff remote rural schools and mission clinics/hospitals (educating leaders and treating mothers/children) [2]; provide drought food aid, boreholes, and orphan scholarships [2]; run vocational carpentry/agriculture centres empowering youth [2].
