a:
(a) 12 J of chemical energy is converted into electrical energy per coulomb of charge driven around the complete circuit [2 marks].
(b) R_total = V/I = 12/3.0 = 4.0 Ω [1 mark]. Since two identical lamps in parallel give half of one lamp: R_single = 2 × 4.0 = 8.0 Ω [2 marks].
p: Physics O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory

q: State Newton's three laws of motion and give one everyday example of Newton's First Law (inertia) in vehicle safety. [5 marks]
a: 1st Law: A body stays at rest or constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force [1]. 2nd Law: Resultant force F = ma (rate of change of momentum) [1]. 3rd Law: For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force [1]. Example: Seatbelts restrain passengers whose inertia tends to keep them moving forward when a car brakes suddenly [2].
p: Physics O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory

q:
A rectangular brick measures 20 cm × 10 cm × 5 cm and weighs 25 N.
(a) Calculate the maximum pressure it can exert on a table (in N/cm² and in Pa). [3 marks]
(b) Calculate the minimum pressure it can exert on the table (in N/cm²). [2 marks]
a:
(a) Maximum pressure occurs on smallest area A = 10 × 5 = 50 cm² (= 0.005 m²). P_max = 25 / 50 = 0.50 N/cm² = 5,000 Pa [3 marks].
(b) Minimum pressure on largest area A = 20 × 10 = 200 cm². P_min = 25 / 200 = 0.125 N/cm² [2 marks].
p: Physics O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory

q:
(a) Draw/describe the truth table of a 2-input NOR gate. [2 marks]
(b) Explain how a thermistor can be used in a potential-divider circuit as an automatic fire alarm trigger. [3 marks]
a:
(a) NOR gate outputs 1 ONLY when both inputs A=0 and B=0; outputs 0 when either or both inputs are 1 [2 marks].
(b) An NTC thermistor's resistance falls sharply as temperature rises; in series with a fixed resistor, voltage across the fixed resistor rises to exceed the threshold switching on the alarm/relay [3 marks].
p: Physics O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory

q: Describe an experiment to measure the specific heat capacity of water using an electrical immersion heater, thermometer, beaker, stopwatch, and joulemeter (or ammeter & voltmeter). [5 marks]
a:
1. Weigh empty insulated beaker and add known mass m of water [1].
2. Record initial water temperature θ₁ [1].
3. Switch on heater, start stopwatch, and record V, I (or joulemeter reading E = VIt) while stirring gently [1].
4. Switch off, stir, and record highest steady temperature θ₂ [1].
5. Compute c = VIt / [m(θ₂ - θ₁)] [1].
p: Physics O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory

q:
An object 2.0 cm tall is placed 15 cm in front of a convex (converging) lens of focal length 10 cm.
(a) Use the lens formula 1/f = 1/u + 1/v to find the image distance v. [3 marks]
(b) State three properties of the image formed (real/virtual, upright/inverted, size). [3 marks]
a:
(a) 1/10 = 1/15 + 1/v -> 1/v = 1/10 - 1/15 = 1/30 -> v = +30 cm [3 marks].
(b) Real, inverted, magnified (magnification = 30/15 = 2×, height 4.0 cm) [3 marks].
p: Physics O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory

q:
A copper rod rests across two bare horizontal rails inside a strong magnetic field directed vertically downwards. When a battery is connected across the rails, the rod rolls sideways.
(a) Name the physical effect demonstrated. [1 mark]
(b) State two ways to increase the force pushing the rod. [2 marks]
(c) State one way to reverse the direction of motion. [1 mark]
a:
(a) The motor effect (force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field) [1 mark].
(b) Increase the electric current; use stronger magnets [2 marks].
(c) Reverse battery polarity (current direction) OR swap N and S magnetic poles [1 mark].
p: Physics O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory

q:
Explain why:
(a) small gaps are left between steel railway tracks, [2 marks]
(b) power lines hang loosely in summer, [2 marks]
(c) double-glazed windows keep rooms warmer in winter. [2 marks]
a:
(a) Allows thermal expansion on hot sunny days so rails do not buckle/bend [2 marks].
(b) Prevents cables snapping under tension when they contract in cold winter nights [2 marks].
(c) Trapped dry air/vacuum between glass panes is a very poor conductor and suppresses convection currents [2 marks].
p: Physics O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory

q:
A stone of mass 0.5 kg is thrown vertically upwards at 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). Neglecting air resistance:
(a) Calculate its initial kinetic energy. [2 marks]
(b) Use conservation of energy to calculate the maximum height reached. [3 marks]
a:
(a) KE = ½mv² = ½ × 0.5 × 20² = 100 J [2 marks].
(b) At max height all KE converts to GPE: mgh = 100 -> 0.5 × 10 × h = 100 -> h = 20 m [3 marks].
p: Physics O-Level Paper 2 — Structured Theory

q: Under IAS 16 (Property, Plant and Equipment), when a non-current asset with a carrying amount of $48,000 is revalued upward to $65,000, how is the $17,000 revaluation surplus initially recognised?
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** Credited to Other Comprehensive Income and accumulated in a Revaluation Reserve in Equity

IAS 16 requires a first-time revaluation surplus to be recognised in Other Comprehensive Income (OCI) and credited to the Revaluation Reserve within Equity (not in profit or loss unless reversing a previous revaluation loss).
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Under IAS 2 (Inventories), inventory items have historical cost $14,200, estimated selling price $15,000, and necessary selling & completion costs of $1,600. At what value must the inventory be stated?
a: NRV = Selling price ($15,000) − Costs to sell ($1,600) = $13,400. IAS 2 mandates inventory be valued at the lower of Cost ($14,200) and NRV ($13,400) = $13,400.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Under IAS 10 (Events after the Reporting Period), a major credit customer owing $22,000 at 31 December 2025 is declared bankrupt on 18 January 2026 before the financial statements are authorised. How is this treated?
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** Adjusting event: write off the irrecoverable debt against 2025 profit and Trade Receivables

A customer bankruptcy soon after year-end normally confirms conditions (credit weakness) already existing at the reporting date, so IAS 10 classifies it as an adjusting event.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Which transaction appears under Cash Flows from Financing Activities in a Statement of Cash Flows prepared under IAS 7?
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** Proceeds from a new issue of ordinary shares and repayment of a 10% debenture loan

IAS 7 defines Financing Activities as those altering the size and composition of contributed equity and borrowings (share issues, share redemptions, debenture/loan receipts & repayments).
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Under IAS 37 (Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets), when a legal claim against a company is judged "possible" (less than 50% probability, not remote), how should it be treated?
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** Disclosed as a contingent liability in the notes to the financial statements

Under IAS 37: Probable (>50%) present obligation = recognise a Provision; Possible obligation = disclose as Contingent Liability in notes; Remote = ignore.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: When a partnership admits a new partner and decides NOT to keep a Goodwill account in the books, how is Goodwill (say $30,000, old PSR 2:1, new PSR 2:2:1) adjusted?
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** Credit old partners in old ratio ($20,000; $10,000) and debit all partners in new ratio ($12,000; $12,000; $6,000)

Raising Goodwill credits old partners in their old PSR; writing off Goodwill debits all partners in the new PSR — resulting in a net transfer from gaining to sacrificing partners.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Under the rule in Garner v Murray upon partnership dissolution when one partner is insolvent, how do the solvent partners share the insolvent partner's capital deficiency?
a: Under Garner v Murray, solvent partners bring in cash equal to their share of realisation loss and bear the insolvent partner's capital deficiency in the ratio of their last agreed capitals.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: A limited company makes a 1-for-4 bonus issue of $1 ordinary shares using Share Premium ($40,000) and Retained Earnings, based on 200,000 existing shares. What happens to Total Equity?
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** Total Equity remains unchanged because reserves are capitalised into Share Capital

Bonus shares are issued free to existing shareholders by transferring reserves to Share Capital (Dr Share Premium/Retained Earnings, Cr Share Capital). Cash and Total Equity do not change.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Why does a manufacturing enterprise create a Provision for Unrealised Profit on manufactured finished goods inventory?
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** To eliminate internal factory profit on unsold goods so closing inventory is stated at production cost in the SOFP

Under prudence/realisation, profit cannot be recognised until goods are sold to an external customer. Eliminating factory mark-up on unsold finished goods prevents overstating inventory and profit.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: A manufacturing company transfers finished goods at cost plus 25% factory mark-up. Unsold finished goods at transfer price increased from $20,000 to $30,000. What is the charge to the Income Statement?
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** $2,000 expense (increase in provision for unrealised profit)

Mark-up 25% on cost = margin 25/125 = 1/5 (20%) on transfer price. Opening PUP = $4,000; Closing PUP = $6,000. Increase = $2,000 debited to Profit or Loss.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Which journal entry records the redemption of $100,000 of redeemable preference shares out of Retained Earnings where no new shares are issued?
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** Dr Preference Share Capital $100k, Cr Bank $100k; and Dr Retained Earnings $100k, Cr Capital Redemption Reserve $100k

When redeemable shares are redeemed without fresh share proceeds, an equivalent sum must be transferred from distributable profits (Retained Earnings) to a non-distributable Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) to maintain capital.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: A company's EPS is $0.45 and market price per ordinary share is $3.60. Calculate the Price/Earnings (P/E) ratio and state what it indicates.
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** 8.0 times — investors pay $8 for each $1 of current annual earnings per share

P/E ratio = Market price per share ÷ EPS = $3.60 ÷ $0.45 = 8.0 times, reflecting market expectations of future earnings growth and risk.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: If a business has Dividend Cover of 2.5 times and Profit After Tax of $125,000 (no preference shares), what total ordinary dividend was declared?
a: Dividend Cover = Profit available to ordinary shareholders ÷ Total Ordinary Dividend. Thus Ordinary Dividend = $125,000 ÷ 2.5 = $50,000.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Under IAS 36 (Impairment of Assets), an asset has carrying amount $90,000, fair value less costs of disposal $72,000, and value in use $78,000. What is the impairment loss?
a: Recoverable amount = higher of Fair Value Less Costs of Disposal ($72,000) and Value in Use ($78,000) = $78,000. Impairment loss = Carrying amount ($90,000) − $78,000 = $12,000.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: In cost accounting, when production volume exceeds sales volume during a period, how does Absorption Costing profit compare with Marginal Costing profit (assuming constant unit costs)?
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** Absorption Costing shows a higher profit because part of fixed production overhead is carried forward in closing inventory

When inventory rises (Production > Sales), Absorption Costing absorbs a share of fixed factory overhead into closing inventory valuation, reducing cost of sales and raising reported profit relative to Marginal Costing.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Standard material per unit is 4 kg at $5/kg. Actual output of 1,000 units used 4,300 kg costing $20,640 (actual price $4.80/kg). What are the Material Price Variance and Material Usage Variance?
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** Price Variance $860 (F); Usage Variance $1,500 (A)

Price variance = AQ(SP − AP) = 4,300($5.00 − $4.80) = $860 Favourable. Usage variance = SP(SQ − AQ) = $5(4,000 − 4,300) = $1,500 Adverse. Net total = $640 Adverse.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Standard labour is 2 hours/unit at $8/hour. Actual output is 500 units taking 950 hours at a total wage cost of $8,075. Calculate the Labour Rate and Labour Efficiency Variances.
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** Rate Variance $475 (A); Efficiency Variance $400 (F)

Standard hours for 500 units = 1,000 hrs. Actual wage cost $8,075 vs standard cost for 950 hrs ($7,600) → Rate Variance = $475 Adverse. Efficiency Variance = $8(1,000 − 950) = $400 Favourable.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: A product sells at $40/unit, variable cost is $24/unit, and fixed costs are $96,000. If actual sales are 8,000 units, what is the Margin of Safety in units and as a percentage of actual sales?
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** 2,000 units (25%)

Contribution/unit = $40 − $24 = $16. Break-even = $96,000 ÷ $16 = 6,000 units. Margin of Safety = 8,000 − 6,000 = 2,000 units; 2,000 ÷ 8,000 = 25%.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Three products require a single scarce machine-hour bottleneck: Product X (Contribution $30, 3 machine hrs), Product Y ($24, 2 machine hrs), Product Z ($28, 4 machine hrs). Which ranking maximises profit?
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** Y ($12/hr), then X ($10/hr), then Z ($7/hr)

With a limiting factor, rank by contribution per unit of scarce resource: Y = $24/2 = $12/hr; X = $30/3 = $10/hr; Z = $28/4 = $7/hr.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: In Capital Investment Appraisal, which statement accurately describes the Internal Rate of Return (IRR)?
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** The discount rate at which the Net Present Value (NPV) of a project equals zero

IRR is the discount rate (cost of capital) where Present Value of cash inflows equals Present Value of cash outflows (NPV = 0). A project is accepted when IRR exceeds the firm's cost of capital.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Under Activity-Based Costing (ABC), what is a "cost driver"?
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** A factor or activity (such as machine setups, purchase orders, or inspections) that causes overhead costs to be incurred

ABC groups overheads into cost pools and assigns them to products using cost drivers—the measurable activities causing each pool's cost to vary.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Under IAS 8 (Accounting Policies, Changes in Accounting Estimates and Errors), how is a change in the useful life of a depreciable machine treated?
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** As a change in accounting estimate: applied prospectively to current and future periods

Changing asset useful life or residual value is a change in accounting estimate (IAS 8) and is accounted for prospectively in current and future periods.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: A company owes $200,000 in 8% debentures and has $300,000 in Share Capital & Reserves. Total Capital Employed is $500,000 and PBIT is $75,000. What are the Capital Gearing Ratio and Interest Cover?
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** Gearing = 40% (Debt/Total Capital Employed); Interest Cover = 4.69 times

Gearing = Fixed-cost capital / Total Capital Employed = $200,000 / $500,000 = 40%. Annual interest = 8% × $200,000 = $16,000. Interest cover = PBIT / Interest = $75,000 / $16,000 = 4.69 times.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Why might a business experience a cash shortage even while reporting strong net profit?
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** Rapid sales growth tied up cash in higher trade receivables and inventory, or heavy capital expenditure and loan repayments occurred

Profit (accrual basis) differs from cash: working capital absorption (rising debtors/stock), asset purchases, tax/dividends paid, and loan repayments reduce cash without lowering operating profit; depreciation reduces profit without using cash.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: In a Make-or-Buy short-term decision where spare capacity exists, which costs are relevant to manufacturing a component in-house?
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** Incremental variable manufacturing costs plus any avoidable specific fixed costs attributable to the component

Only future, incremental, differential cash flows (direct materials, direct labour, variable overhead, avoidable fixed costs, and any opportunity cost) are relevant; sunk and general absorbed fixed costs are irrelevant.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Under IAS 38 (Intangible Assets), how must internal Research expenditure versus qualifying Development expenditure be treated?
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** Expense Research costs immediately in profit or loss; capitalise Development costs only if all six strict IAS 38 commercial/technical feasibility criteria are met

IAS 38 requires all Research expenditure to be expensed as incurred, while Development expenditure is capitalised as an intangible asset only when technical feasibility, intention/ability to use or sell, probable future benefits, resources, and reliable measurement are demonstrated.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: A machine costs $50,000 (no residual value, 5-year life). Annual net cash inflows are $16,000. What is the Accounting Rate of Return (ARR) based on initial investment?
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** 12% [($16,000 − $10,000 depreciation) = $6,000 average profit ÷ $50,000]

Annual depreciation = $50,000 ÷ 5 = $10,000. Average accounting profit = Cash flow ($16,000) − Depreciation ($10,000) = $6,000/yr. ARR = ($6,000 ÷ $50,000) × 100% = 12%.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Budgeted fixed production overhead was $60,000 for 12,000 budgeted labour hours (10,000 units). Actual output was 10,500 units using 12,400 hours and actual fixed overhead was $61,500. What is the Fixed Overhead Expenditure Variance?
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** $1,500 Adverse ($60,000 budgeted − $61,500 actual)

Fixed Overhead Expenditure Variance = Budgeted Fixed Overhead ($60,000) − Actual Fixed Overhead ($61,500) = $1,500 Adverse (overspent).
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: In budgetary control, why is a Flexible Budget essential for performance evaluation?
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** It adjusts budgeted variable costs and revenues to the actual level of activity achieved so true operational efficiency variances are isolated

Comparing actual costs at 12,000 units against a static budget for 10,000 units mixes volume changes with efficiency. Flexing the budget to 12,000 units isolates real price/efficiency performance.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: In incomplete records, opening inventory is $18,000, closing inventory is $22,000, purchases are $124,000, and sales achieve a uniform 20% gross profit margin on sales. Calculate Total Sales.
a: Cost of goods sold = $18,000 + $124,000 − $22,000 = $120,000. Since Margin = 20% of Sales, COGS = 80% of Sales → Sales = $120,000 ÷ 0.80 = $150,000.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Chipo and Tatenda share profits in the ratio 3:2 with capitals of $60,000 and $40,000. On 1 January, Nyasha is admitted for a 1/5 share in future profits, contributing $35,000 capital. Goodwill is valued at $25,000 (not to remain in the books), and Premises are revalued upward by $15,000. Calculate each partner's final Capital Account balance.
a:
### Step 1: Revaluation Profit (Old Ratio 3:2) [3 marks]
- Chipo: 3/5 × $15,000 = $9,000
- Tatenda: 2/5 × $15,000 = $6,000

### Step 2: New Profit-Sharing Ratio & Goodwill Adjustment [5 marks]
- Remaining share = 1 − 1/5 = 4/5 → Chipo 12/25 (48%), Tatenda 8/25 (32%), Nyasha 5/25 (20%).
- Credit Goodwill in old ratio (3:2): Chipo +$15,000, Tatenda +$10,000.
- Debit Goodwill in new ratio (12:8:5): Chipo −$12,000, Tatenda −$8,000, Nyasha −$5,000.

### Step 3: Closing Capital Balances [4 marks]
- **Chipo:** $60,000 + $9,000 + $15,000 − $12,000 = **$72,000**
- **Tatenda:** $40,000 + $6,000 + $10,000 − $8,000 = **$48,000**
- **Nyasha:** $35,000 − $5,000 = **$30,000** [Total: 12 marks]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: Under IAS 7, extract Operating Profit before Working Capital Changes and Net Cash from Operating Activities from: Profit before tax $84,000; Depreciation $18,000; Loss on disposal of equipment $3,500; Finance cost $6,000 (all paid in cash); Inventory increased by $9,000; Trade Receivables decreased by $4,500; Trade Payables increased by $5,000; Income tax paid $16,000.
a:
### IAS 7 Cash Flow Operating Section [10 marks]
1. **Profit before tax:** $84,000
2. **Adjustments for non-cash & financing items:**
   - Add Depreciation: +$18,000 [1 mark]
   - Add Loss on disposal: +$3,500 [1 mark]
   - Add Finance cost: +$6,000 [1 mark]
   - Operating cash flow before working capital = **$111,500** [1 mark]
3. **Working capital changes:**
   - Increase in Inventory: ($9,000) [1 mark]
   - Decrease in Trade Receivables: +$4,500 [1 mark]
   - Increase in Trade Payables: +$5,000 [1 mark]
   - Cash generated from operations = **$112,000** [1 mark]
4. **Less:** Interest paid ($6,000) and Tax paid ($16,000) [1 mark]
5. **Net Cash Inflow from Operating Activities = $90,000** [1 mark]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: A limited company has 400,000 $0.50 ordinary shares ($200,000), Share Premium $30,000, Revaluation Reserve $40,000, and Retained Earnings $110,000 at 1 Jan. During the year: (1) Issued 100,000 shares at $0.85; (2) Made a 1-for-5 bonus issue out of Share Premium first, then Retained Earnings; (3) Revalued land upward by $25,000; (4) Earned Profit for the year $68,000 and paid dividends of $18,000. Prepare the Statement of Changes in Equity.
a:
### Statement of Changes in Equity [12 marks]
- **1 Jan Balances:** Share Capital $200,000 | Share Premium $30,000 | Reval Reserve $40,000 | Retained Earnings $110,000 | **Total $380,000** [2 marks]
- **Issue of 100,000 shares at $0.85:** Share Capital +$50,000; Share Premium +$35,000 (+$85,000 Total) [3 marks]
- **1-for-5 Bonus Issue:** Total shares now 500,000 → 100,000 bonus shares of $0.50 = $50,000. Uses Share Premium ($50,000 out of $65,000 available, leaving $15,000), Share Capital +$50,000 (Net Total $0) [3 marks]
- **Revaluation OCI:** Reval Reserve +$25,000 [1 mark]
- **Profit $68,000 & Dividends ($18,000):** Retained Earnings +$50,000 [2 marks]
- **Closing Totals (31 Dec):** Share Capital **$300,000** | Share Premium **$15,000** | Reval Reserve **$65,000** | Retained Earnings **$160,000** | **Total Equity $540,000** [1 mark]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: During audit of Mutare Wholesalers, net profit was draft $52,400 and a Suspense credit balance of $1,340 existed. Errors found: (a) Sales day book was undercast by $900; (b) Discount allowed $260 was credited to Discount Received; (c) Purchase of repairs $1,200 was debited to Machinery Account (depreciation 10% straight-line charged); (d) Credit note to a customer $320 was omitted from both ledgers. Show journal entries to clear Suspense and compute corrected Net Profit.
a:
### Journal Adjustments & Revised Profit [12 marks]
- **(a)** Dr Suspense $900 / Cr Sales $900 → Profit **+$900** [2 marks]
- **(b)** Dr Discount Allowed $260, Dr Discount Received $260 / Cr Suspense $520 → Profit **−$520** [3 marks]
- **(c)** Dr Repairs $1,200 / Cr Machinery $1,200 → Profit **−$1,200**; Reverse excess depreciation: Dr Accum Dep $120 / Cr Dep Expense $120 → Profit **+$120** [3 marks]
- **(d)** Dr Sales Returns $320 / Cr Trade Receivables $320 (no suspense impact) → Profit **−$320** [2 marks]
- **Suspense check:** Cr $1,340 + Cr $520 (wait: if Suspense started Cr $1,340? Check net suspense: (a) Dr 900, (b) Cr 520 → net Dr 380; opening balance would have been Cr $380 to clear, note exact entry logic awarded method marks) [1 mark]
- **Corrected Net Profit:** $52,400 + $900 − $520 − $1,200 + $120 − $320 = **$51,380** [1 mark]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: Mbare Manufacturing produces goods transferred to finished warehouse at production cost plus 20%. Data: Raw materials consumed $95,000; Direct labour $62,000; Direct expenses $8,000; Factory overheads $45,000; Opening WIP $14,000; Closing WIP $19,000; Opening finished goods at transfer price $24,000; Closing finished goods at transfer price $36,000. Prepare the Manufacturing Account and calculate the Provision for Unrealised Profit adjustment.
a:
### Manufacturing Account & PUP [10 marks]
1. **Prime Cost:** $95,000 + $62,000 + $8,000 = **$165,000** [2 marks]
2. **Add Factory Overheads:** $165,000 + $45,000 = $210,000 [1 mark]
3. **Adjust WIP:** +$14,000 − $19,000 = **Production Cost = $205,000** [2 marks]
4. **Add 20% Factory Profit:** $205,000 × 20% = **+$41,000** → **Transfer Value = $246,000** [2 marks]
5. **PUP Adjustment:** 20/120 = 1/6 of transfer price. Opening PUP = $24,000/6 = $4,000; Closing PUP = $36,000/6 = $6,000. Increase in PUP = **$2,000** charged against Profit or Loss [3 marks]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: Explain clearly how IAS 16 differs from IAS 40 (Investment Property) in accounting for subsequent measurement gains on buildings held for capital appreciation versus owner-occupied factory buildings.
a:
### IAS 16 vs IAS 40 [8 marks]
- **Owner-Occupied (IAS 16):** Cost Model or Revaluation Model. Revaluation gains go to **Other Comprehensive Income** and Revaluation Reserve in Equity (not Profit or Loss, unless reversing an earlier downward loss); asset continues to be depreciated over useful life [4 marks].
- **Investment Property (IAS 40):** Cost Model or **Fair Value Model**. Under Fair Value Model, changes in fair value are recognised **directly in Profit or Loss** each year, and the property is **not depreciated** [4 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: Harare Sports Club had Subscriptions received in cash $18,400 during 2025. At 1 Jan 2025: Subscriptions in arrears $1,200, in advance $900. At 31 Dec 2025: Arrears $1,650 (of which $250 from 2024 are written off as irrecoverable), in advance $1,400. Bar takings were $22,000, opening bar inventory $1,800, closing bar inventory $2,300, bar purchases $13,200, bar steward wages $3,100. Calculate (a) Subscriptions Income for 2025 and (b) Bar Profit.
a:
### (a) Subscriptions Account [6 marks]
- Cash received: $18,400
- Less Opening Arrears ($1,200) [written off $250 appears as separate Irrecoverable Subscriptions expense in I&E; recoverable 2024 cash = $950]
- Add Opening Advance: +$900
- Add Closing Arrears: +$1,400 (remaining valid 2025 arrears: $1,650 − $250 written off)
- Less Closing Advance: ($1,400)
- **Subscriptions Income to Income & Expenditure = $18,100** (and Bad Subscriptions written off = $250)

### (b) Bar Trading Account [4 marks]
- Bar Sales $22,000 − COGS ($1,800 + $13,200 − $2,300 = $12,700) − Wages ($3,100) = **Bar Profit = $6,200** [Total: 10 marks]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: A retail trader keeps single-entry records. Net Assets were $45,000 on 1 Jan and $63,500 on 31 Dec. During the year the owner took $750/month cash drawings, $1,800 goods at cost for family use, and introduced $10,000 private capital. Compute Net Profit for the year and explain two limitations of deriving profit from a Statement of Affairs.
a:
### Statement of Profit [6 marks]
- Closing Capital $63,500 − Opening Capital $45,000 = Net Increase $18,500
- Add Drawings: Cash ($750 × 12 = $9,000) + Goods ($1,800) = +$10,800
- Less Capital Introduced: ($10,000)
- **Net Profit = $19,300** [4 marks]

### Limitations of Single Entry [4 marks]
1. No detailed breakdown of Gross Profit, Sales, Expenses, or Margins for management control.
2. Higher risk of undetected arithmetic/fraud errors without a double-entry Trial Balance [Total: 8 marks]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: Given Trade Receivables at 31 Dec $140,000, Specific Bad Debts to write off $4,000, General Allowance for Doubtful Debts 5%, and Opening Allowance $7,500: (a) Calculate the Income Statement net charge or credit for Bad & Doubtful Debts and (b) Show the SOFP Net Trade Receivables.
a:
### Bad & Doubtful Debts [8 marks]
- Trade Receivables after specific write-off = $140,000 − $4,000 = **$136,000** [2 marks]
- Required Closing Allowance = 5% × $136,000 = **$6,800** [2 marks]
- Decrease in Allowance = $7,500 − $6,800 = **$700 Credit** to Income Statement [2 marks]
- Net Income Statement Expense = Bad Debt $4,000 − Reduction $700 = **$3,300 Expense** [1 mark]
- **SOFP Net Trade Receivables = $136,000 − $6,800 = $129,200** [1 mark]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: Two companies Alpha and Beta have identical ROCE of 18%, yet Alpha has Gross Margin 40% & Net Margin 6% with Asset Turnover 3.0×, while Beta has Gross Margin 25% & Net Margin 15% with Asset Turnover 1.2×. Compare their business models and financial risk.
a:
### Comparative Ratio Interpretation [10 marks]
- **Alpha (High-Volume / Supermarket Model):** Low net profit margin (6%) compensated by rapid asset utilisation (3.0× turnover) → ROCE = 6% × 3.0 = 18%. However, big gap between 40% Gross Margin and 6% Net Margin highlights heavy operating/distribution overhead [5 marks].
- **Beta (Low-Volume / Specialist Model):** Tighter overhead control retains 15% Net Margin out of 25% Gross Margin, turning assets more slowly (1.2×) → 15% × 1.2 = 18%. Lower sensitivity to price discounting than Alpha [5 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: Explain three purposes of IAS 2 Inventories and show the effect on both Year 1 and Year 2 net profit if closing inventory at the end of Year 1 is overstated by $12,000.
a:
### IAS 2 & Inventory Error Effect [8 marks]
- **Purposes of IAS 2:** Standardise cost formulas (FIFO / AVCO), enforce prudent lower-of-cost-and-NRV valuation, and ensure consistent financial comparability [4 marks].
- **Error Impact:** Year 1 closing inventory overstated by $12,000 → Year 1 Cost of Sales understated → **Year 1 Net Profit overstated by $12,000** [2 marks]. Year 1 closing becomes Year 2 opening inventory → Year 2 Cost of Sales overstated → **Year 2 Net Profit understated by $12,000** (self-cancelling over two years) [2 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: A business owns Machinery (cost $120,000, accumulated depreciation $54,000 on 1 Jan). On 1 July, a machine originally costing $30,000 (accumulated depreciation $18,000 at 1 Jan) is sold for $9,500. Depreciation is 20% p.a. reducing balance, charged proportionately in the year of sale/purchase. Calculate (a) Disposal Gain/Loss and (b) Total Depreciation Expense for the year.
a:
### Non-Current Asset Disposal & Depreciation [10 marks]
- **Sold machine carrying amount on 1 Jan:** $30,000 − $18,000 = $12,000 [1 mark]
- **6 months depreciation to 1 July:** 20% × $12,000 × 6/12 = **$1,200** → Carrying amount at sale = **$10,800** [3 marks]
- **Disposal Outcome:** Proceeds $9,500 − $10,800 = **Loss on Disposal $1,300** [2 marks]
- **Remaining machinery depreciation (full year):** Remaining cost $90,000, Acc Dep ($54,000 − $18,000 = $36,000) → Carrying amount $54,000 × 20% = **$10,800** [3 marks]
- **Total Depreciation Charge = $1,200 + $10,800 = $12,000** [1 mark]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: Outline the difference between Capital Reserve and Revenue Reserve with two examples of each, and explain how each affects dividend distribution under company law.
a:
### Capital vs Revenue Reserves [8 marks]
- **Capital Reserves:** Non-distributable as cash dividends because they arise from capital transactions or unrealised gains (e.g., **Share Premium, Revaluation Reserve, Capital Redemption Reserve**). May be used for bonus share issues [4 marks].
- **Revenue Reserves:** Created from realised operating profits and are legally distributable as cash dividends (e.g., **Retained Earnings, General Reserve**) [4 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: A company issues 500,000 $1 ordinary shares on 1 Jan (cash received), issues $200,000 10% debentures on 1 April (interest payable half-yearly on 30 Sept and 31 March), and declares/pays an interim ordinary dividend of $0.06/share on 1 August. Compute Finance Cost and Dividend Equity Charge in the year's financial statements.
a:
### Debentures Interest & Equity Dividends [8 marks]
- **Debenture Interest (1 April – 31 Dec = 9 months):** 10% × $200,000 × 9/12 = **$15,000** charged to Statement of Profit or Loss ($10,000 paid on 30 Sept; **$5,000 accrued** at 31 Dec as a current liability) [5 marks].
- **Interim Dividend Paid:** 500,000 × $0.06 = **$30,000** debited to Retained Earnings in Statement of Changes in Equity (NOT an expense in Profit or Loss) [3 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: Explain why the ethical principles of Objectivity, Professional Competence, and Confidentiality are essential for external auditors and company accountants in Zimbabwe.
a:
### Accounting Ethics [8 marks]
- **Objectivity:** Prevents bias or conflict of interest when valuing assets, provisions, or goodwill [2–3 marks].
- **Professional Competence & Due Care:** Ensures IFRS/IAS standards and tax rules are accurately applied without negligence [2–3 marks].
- **Confidentiality:** Protects sensitive corporate client strategies and payroll data unless legally required to disclose [2–3 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: A partnership agreement states: Interest on capital 8% p.a., Partner A salary $12,000/yr, Interest on drawings 10% p.a., Residual profits shared 2:1. Capitals: A $50,000, B $30,000. Drawings taken mid-year: A $10,000, B $8,000. Profit for the year before appropriation is $45,100. Prepare the Appropriation Account.
a:
### Partnership Appropriation Account [10 marks]
- Profit for the year: **$45,100**
- **Add Interest on Drawings (6 months average):** A: 10% × $10,000 × 6/12 = $500; B: 10% × $8,000 × 6/12 = $400 → Total **+$900** → Available = **$46,000** [3 marks]
- **Less Appropriations:**
  - Salary A: $12,000 [1 mark]
  - Interest on Capital: A $4,000 (8% × $50k), B $2,400 (8% × $30k) = $6,400 [2 marks]
  - Residual Profit = $46,000 − $18,400 = **$27,600** [1 mark]
- **Share of Residual Profit (2:1):** A = **$18,400**, B = **$9,200** [3 marks]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: State and explain three differences between a Non-Profit Organisation's Receipts & Payments Account and its Income & Expenditure Account.
a:
### Receipts & Payments vs Income & Expenditure [6 marks]
1. **Basis:** Receipts & Payments is cash-based (summary of cashbook); Income & Expenditure uses accruals & matching [2 marks].
2. **Capital vs Revenue:** R&P includes capital receipts/expenditure (e.g., buying equipment); I&E includes only revenue items plus depreciation [2 marks].
3. **Closing Balance:** R&P ends with closing cash/bank balance; I&E calculates annual Surplus or Deficit [2 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: A business has Current Ratio 2.4:1, Acid-Test (Quick) Ratio 0.8:1, and Current Liabilities of $50,000. Calculate (a) Total Current Assets, (b) Closing Inventory value, and (c) Evaluate the company's short-term liquidity.
a:
### Working Capital & Liquidity Ratios [8 marks]
- **(a) Current Assets:** 2.4 × $50,000 = **$120,000** [2 marks]
- **(b) Liquid Assets (CA − Inventory):** 0.8 × $50,000 = $40,000 → **Closing Inventory = $120,000 − $40,000 = $80,000** [3 marks]
- **(c) Evaluation:** Current Ratio appears healthy (2.4:1), but Acid-Test of 0.8:1 (< 1.0 benchmark) reveals excessive capital locked in slow-moving inventory ($80k = 67% of current assets), creating short-term cash squeeze risk [3 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: On 1 July 2025, Kwekwe Motors sold a truck on consignment to Bulawayo Agents: 10 units at cost $12,000 each; consignor paid freight $6,000. Bulawayo Agents sold 7 units at $16,500 each, paid selling expenses $2,100, and earns 5% commission on gross sales. Compute Consignment Profit and Closing Inventory Valuation.
a:
### Consignment Account [10 marks]
- **Total landed cost per unit:** ($120,000 + $6,000 freight) ÷ 10 = **$12,600/unit** [2 marks]
- **Closing inventory (3 unsold units):** 3 × $12,600 = **$37,800** [2 marks]
- **Gross Sales (7 units):** 7 × $16,500 = **$115,500** [1 mark]
- **Less Costs:** Landed cost of 7 units ($88,200) + Agent expenses ($2,100) + Commission (5% × $115,500 = $5,775) = $96,075 [3 marks]
- **Consignment Net Profit = $115,500 − $96,075 = $19,425** [2 marks]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: Contrast how Trade Receivables Turnover (days) and Trade Payables Turnover (days) together determine a firm's Working Capital Cash Conversion Cycle, explaining one practical danger of stretching Trade Payables excessively.
a:
### Cash Conversion Cycle [8 marks]
- **Cycle Formula:** Inventory Days + Receivables Collection Days − Payables Payment Days = Cash Conversion Cycle (days cash is tied up before customer collection) [4 marks].
- **Danger of Excessive Payables Stretching:** Straining supplier goodwill may cause loss of early settlement discounts, tighter credit limits, supply interruptions, or late-payment penalty charges [4 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 2 — Structured Questions

q: Standard cost per unit of Product P is: Material 5 kg @ $4/kg = $20; Labour 3 hrs @ $9/hr = $27; Variable overhead 3 hrs @ $2/hr = $6. Actual output of 2,000 units used 10,400 kg costing $39,520 and 5,800 labour hours costing $55,100 (actual variable overhead $12,180). Compute (a) Material Price & Usage, (b) Labour Rate & Efficiency, and (c) Variable Overhead Expenditure & Efficiency Variances.
a:
### Complete Variance Schedule [12 marks]
- **Material Price:** 10,400($4.00 − $3.80) = **$2,080 (F)** [2 marks]
- **Material Usage:** $4(10,000 − 10,400) = **$1,600 (A)** [2 marks]
- **Labour Rate:** 5,800($9.00 − $9.50) = **$2,900 (A)** [2 marks]
- **Labour Efficiency:** $9(6,000 − 5,800) = **$1,800 (F)** [2 marks]
- **Variable Overhead Expenditure:** (5,800 × $2) − $12,180 = **$580 (A)** [2 marks]
- **Variable Overhead Efficiency:** $2(6,000 − 5,800) = **$400 (F)** [2 marks]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: A factory produces 10,000 units in Month 1 and sells 8,500 units at $50/unit. Variable production cost is $22/unit, Fixed production overhead is $80,000 (budgeted output 10,000 units → OAR $8/unit), and fixed selling cost is $35,000. Prepare summarised Profit Statements under (a) Marginal Costing and (b) Absorption Costing, and reconcile the difference.
a:
### Marginal vs Absorption Profit Reconciliation [12 marks]
- **Marginal Costing:** Sales $425,000 − Variable COGS (8,500 × $22 = $187,000) = Contribution $238,000. Less Total Fixed Costs ($80,000 + $35,000 = $115,000) = **Net Profit $123,000** [5 marks].
- **Absorption Costing:** Full production cost/unit = $22 + $8 = $30. COGS = 8,500 × $30 = $255,000. Gross Profit = $170,000 − Fixed Selling $35,000 = **Net Profit $135,000** [5 marks].
- **Reconciliation:** Inventory increase (1,500 units) × Fixed OAR ($8/unit) = **$12,000** higher profit under Absorption Costing ($123,000 + $12,000 = $135,000) [2 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: Three products A, B, C have selling prices $60, $50, $45; variable costs $36, $32, $33; and require scarce skilled labour hours of 4 hrs, 2 hrs, and 1.5 hrs respectively. Maximum monthly demand is 400 A, 500 B, and 600 C. Available skilled labour is strictly 2,400 hours. Determine the profit-maximising production plan and maximum total contribution.
a:
### Limiting Factor Optimisation [12 marks]
1. **Contribution/unit:** A = $24; B = $18; C = $12 [2 marks]
2. **Contribution per scarce labour hour:**
   - A: $24 ÷ 4 = $6.00/hr (Rank 3)
   - B: $18 ÷ 2 = **$9.00/hr (Rank 1)**
   - C: $12 ÷ 1.5 = **$8.00/hr (Rank 2)** [4 marks]
3. **Allocation of 2,400 hours:**
   - Make 500 B (1,000 hrs) → Contribution = **$9,000**
   - Make 600 C (900 hrs) → Contribution = **$7,200**
   - Remaining 500 hrs ÷ 4 = **125 units of A** → Contribution = **$3,000** [4 marks]
4. **Maximum Total Contribution = $19,200** [2 marks]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: Gweru Engineering currently manufactures 2,000 brackets/year in-house: Direct materials $18/unit, Direct labour $12/unit, Variable overhead $5/unit, Fixed supervisor salary (avoidable if outsourced) $16,000/yr, Apportioned general factory rent $24,000/yr. An external supplier offers to supply 2,000 brackets at $41/unit. Advise management quantitatively and state two non-financial factors.
a:
### Make-or-Buy Decision [10 marks]
- **Relevant In-House Cost:** Variable cost 2,000 × ($18 + $12 + $5 = $35) = $70,000 + Avoidable supervisor salary $16,000 = **$86,000** ($43.00/unit). Apportioned general rent ($24,000) is irrelevant [4 marks].
- **External Purchase Cost:** 2,000 × $41 = **$82,000** [2 marks]
- **Financial Advice:** Outsource to save **$4,000/year** [1 mark].
- **Non-financial factors:** Supplier quality reliability/lead times, workforce morale if redundancies occur, and potential alternative use of freed factory space [3 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: A project requires an immediate capital outlay of $150,000 (scrap value $10,000 at Year 4) and generates annual net cash inflows of $52,000 for 4 years. Cost of capital is 10% (Discount factors: Yr1 0.909, Yr2 0.826, Yr3 0.751, Yr4 0.683). Calculate (a) Payback Period and (b) Net Present Value (NPV), advising whether to accept.
a:
### Capital Investment Appraisal [10 marks]
- **(a) Payback Period:** $150,000 ÷ $52,000 = **2.88 years** (2 yrs 11 months) [3 marks]
- **(b) NPV Calculation:**
  - Annuity factor (10%, 4 yrs) = 0.909 + 0.826 + 0.751 + 0.683 = **3.169**
  - PV of operating inflows = $52,000 × 3.169 = **$164,788** [3 marks]
  - PV of Year 4 scrap value = $10,000 × 0.683 = **$6,830** [2 marks]
  - Less Initial Outlay ($150,000) → **NPV = +$21,618** [1 mark]
- **Decision:** Accept project as NPV is positive (+$21,618), increasing shareholder wealth [1 mark].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: Budgeted sales for Jan–Mar are $80,000, $90,000, $110,000 (30% cash sales with 5% discount; 70% credit collected 60% in the following month and 40% two months after sale; November credit sales $42,000, December credit sales $49,000). Purchases are $55,000/month paid one month after purchase. Wages are $18,000/month paid in the month incurred. Opening cash 1 Jan is $12,000. Prepare the Cash Budget for January and February.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: A machine department has budgeted overhead $120,000 and 15,000 budgeted machine hours. Product Alpha takes 2 machine hours/unit and Product Beta takes 4 machine hours/unit. Under Activity-Based Costing, $120,000 splits into: Machine power $60,000 (15,000 hrs), Setup costs $40,000 (100 setups: Alpha 60, Beta 40), and Quality inspection $20,000 (200 inspections: Alpha 150, Beta 50) for outputs of 3,500 Alpha and 2,000 Beta. Compare overhead per unit under Traditional vs ABC.
a:
### Traditional Absorption vs ABC [12 marks]
- **Traditional OAR:** $120,000 ÷ 15,000 hrs = **$8/hr** → Alpha = **$16/unit**, Beta = **$32/unit** [3 marks]
- **ABC Cost Driver Rates:** Power $4/hr; Setup $400/setup; Inspection $100/inspection [3 marks]
- **Alpha ABC Total:** Power (7,000×$4=$28,000) + Setups (60×$400=$24,000) + Insp (150×$100=$15,000) = $67,000 ÷ 3,500 = **$19.14/unit** (Traditional under-costed Alpha!) [3 marks]
- **Beta ABC Total:** Power (8,000×$4=$32,000) + Setups (40×$400=$16,000) + Insp (50×$100=$5,000) = $53,000 ÷ 2,000 = **$26.50/unit** (Traditional over-costed Beta!) [3 marks]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: A company uses an overhead absorption rate based on 10,000 budgeted labour hours and $150,000 budgeted fixed overhead. Actual hours worked were 10,800 and actual fixed overhead incurred was $158,000. Calculate over- or under-absorption of overhead and explain how it is adjusted in the Statement of Profit or Loss.
a:
### Over/Under Absorption [8 marks]
- **Predetermined OAR:** $150,000 ÷ 10,000 = **$15/labour hour** [2 marks]
- **Overhead Absorbed:** 10,800 actual hours × $15 = **$162,000** [2 marks]
- **Variance:** Absorbed ($162,000) − Actual ($158,000) = **$4,000 Over-absorbed** [2 marks]
- **Adjustment:** Over-absorbed overhead means too much cost was charged to Cost of Sales, so **$4,000 is credited/added back** to Gross Profit in the Statement of Profit or Loss [2 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: Explain the meaning and purpose of a Master Budget, distinguishing between the Operating Budget and the Financial Budget, and discuss two behavioural drawbacks of imposing top-down budgets.
a:
### Master Budgeting & Behavioural Issues [8 marks]
- **Structure:** Master Budget consolidates Operating Budgets (sales, production, materials, labour) and Financial Budgets (cash budget, budgeted Income Statement & SOFP) [4 marks].
- **Top-down drawbacks:** (1) Low staff motivation/ownership due to lack of participation; (2) Budgetary slack or short-term gaming ("spend-it-or-lose-it" mindset) if targets feel unachievable [4 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: A company produces and sells two products in a fixed sales mix of 2 units of S (contribution $15/unit) to 1 unit of L (contribution $30/unit). Total fixed costs are $180,000. Calculate the weighted-average contribution per mix and the break-even sales volume for each product.
a:
### Multi-Product Break-Even [8 marks]
- **Contribution per mix (2S + 1L):** (2 × $15) + (1 × $30) = **$60 per mix** [3 marks]
- **Break-even mixes:** $180,000 ÷ $60 = **3,000 mixes** [2 marks]
- **Break-even units:** **6,000 units of S** and **3,000 units of L** (total 9,000 units) [3 marks]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: Normal capacity is 12,000 units/year; current sales are 9,000 units at $40/unit (variable cost $24/unit, fixed cost $90,000/yr). A one-off export customer offers to buy 2,000 extra units at $29/unit, requiring special export packaging of $2/unit. Should management accept the special order?
a:
### Special Order Decision [8 marks]
- **Relevant Revenue:** 2,000 × $29 = **$58,000** [2 marks]
- **Relevant Incremental Cost:** 2,000 × ($24 + $2 packaging) = **$52,000** (Fixed cost $90,000 is unchanged within capacity) [3 marks]
- **Incremental Profit:** **+$6,000** [1 mark]
- **Advice:** Accept financially, provided existing domestic customers paying $40 do not demand similar $29 discounts (brand/market segmentation check) [2 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: Using EOQ (Economic Order Quantity), annual demand D = 16,000 units, ordering cost C₀ = $45 per order, holding cost Cₕ = $3.60 per unit per year. Calculate (a) the optimal EOQ and (b) the total annual ordering and holding cost at EOQ.
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: At 60% capacity (3,000 units), total cost is $74,000; at 90% capacity (4,500 units), total cost is $98,000. Using the High-Low method, separate variable cost per unit and total fixed cost, then budget total cost at 80% capacity (4,000 units).
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: A division reports controllable profit $96,000 on divisional net assets of $400,000. Group cost of capital is 15%. A new manager is offered a project earning 19% return on $100,000 investment. Compare how the manager reacts under Return on Investment (ROI) versus Residual Income (RI).
a:
### ROI vs Residual Income [8 marks]
- **Current ROI:** $96,000 ÷ $400,000 = **24%** [1 mark]
- **Under ROI:** Project yields 19% (< 24%), pulling divisional ROI down to ($96k+$19k)/$500k = 23%. Manager using ROI rejects a project that actually benefits the group (>15%) — dysfunctional behaviour! [4 marks]
- **Under RI:** Project earns $19,000 profit − (15% × $100,000 = $15,000 imputed interest) = **+$4,000 positive RI**. Manager accepts, achieving goal congruence [3 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: In Process Costing, 1,000 kg of material costing $8,200 plus conversion costs of $3,800 enter Process 1. Normal loss is 10% (scrap value $1.50/kg). Actual good output is 880 kg. Calculate (a) cost per good unit, (b) value of abnormal loss, and (c) Prepare the Process 1 Account.
a:
### Process Costing with Abnormal Loss [10 marks]
- **Expected output:** 1,000 − 100 (normal loss) = **900 kg** [1 mark]
- **Normal loss scrap recovery:** 100 kg × $1.50 = **$150** [1 mark]
- **Net process cost:** ($8,200 + $3,800) − $150 = **$11,850** [2 marks]
- **Cost per kg:** $11,850 ÷ 900 = **$13.17/kg** [2 marks]
- **Abnormal Loss:** 900 − 880 = 20 kg × $13.17 = **$263**; **Good output (880 kg):** $11,587 (total balanced $12,000) [4 marks]
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: A project yields NPV of +$14,000 at 10% and −$6,000 at 18%. Use linear interpolation to calculate its Internal Rate of Return (IRR).
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: Product Line Z generates Sales $90,000, Variable Costs $55,000, Direct Attributable Fixed Costs $28,000, and Allocated Head-Office Overhead $15,000 (currently showing an accounting "loss" of $8,000). Advise whether Line Z should be closed.
a:
### Segment Shutdown Analysis [8 marks]
- **Contribution:** $90,000 − $55,000 = **$35,000** [2 marks]
- **Less Avoidable Specific Fixed Costs:** $35,000 − $28,000 = **+$7,000 net positive contribution** to general overheads [3 marks]
- **Advice:** Do NOT shut down Line Z because closing it removes $7,000 towards unavoidable head-office costs ($15,000), worsening total company profit by $7,000 [3 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: Compare Batch Costing and Job Costing, giving one practical Zimbabwean industry example for each and explaining how Selling Price is determined using a 25% mark-up versus a 25% margin.
a:
### Job vs Batch Costing & Pricing [8 marks]
- **Job Costing:** Costs tracked per unique one-off customer order (e.g., bespoke wedding furniture, commercial audit) [2 marks].
- **Batch Costing:** Costs accumulated for a homogeneous group of identical units, divided by batch size (e.g., bakery loaves, shoe batches, pharmaceuticals) [2 marks].
- **Pricing on Cost $120:** 25% Mark-up = $120 × 1.25 = **$150**; 25% Margin = $120 ÷ 0.75 = **$160** [4 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: Distinguish between Zero-Based Budgeting (ZBB) and Incremental Budgeting, highlighting two advantages and one limitation of ZBB for a local municipality.
a:
### ZBB vs Incremental Budgeting [8 marks]
- **Incremental:** Starts from prior period's budget and adds inflation/percentage adjustments (quick, but perpetuates historical waste) [2 marks].
- **ZBB:** Every activity starts from zero and must justify its cost-benefit case from scratch each cycle [2 marks].
- **Advantages:** Eliminates legacy inefficiency; aligns funding strictly to priority services. **Limitation:** Extremely time-consuming and costly in management hours [4 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: Explain what is meant by "Capital Rationing" (distinguishing Soft vs Hard capital rationing) and show how Profitability Index (PI = NPV / Initial Outlay) ranks divisible projects.
a:
### Capital Rationing & Profitability Index [8 marks]
- **Soft Rationing:** Internal management-imposed investment caps (e.g., reluctance to dilute equity or issue debt). **Hard Rationing:** External bank/market refusal to lend capital [4 marks].
- **Profitability Index:** When capital is constrained, divide NPV (or PV of inflows) by Dollar Investment to maximise NPV generated per $1 invested across divisible projects [4 marks].
p: Accounting A-Level Paper 3 — Problem Solving

q: Which measure is most useful for comparing the efficiency of two farm enterprises that use different amounts of variable inputs?

q: Which soil property most directly determines the soil's ability to resist a rapid change in pH when acid or alkali is added?

a:
**Correct Answer (D):** It regulates gas exchange and water loss

Stomata regulate CO2 entry for photosynthesis and water-vapour loss through transpiration.

The threshold supports economically justified intervention rather than automatic pesticide application.

q: What does heritability describe in quantitative genetics?
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** The proportion of observed phenotypic variation attributable to genetic variation in a specified population and environment

Heritability is a population statistic describing the genetic contribution to phenotypic variance under specified conditions.
p: Agriculture A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Which amino-acid-related concept is central when assessing the quality of protein in a monogastric animal diet?
a: The limiting essential amino acid constrains the utilisation of other amino acids for protein synthesis.

q: Which hormone is strongly associated with milk ejection in a lactating mammal?
a: Oxytocin stimulates contraction of myoepithelial cells, causing milk ejection.

q: What is a major advantage of including a well-managed legume in a pasture system?
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** Biological nitrogen fixation can increase nitrogen inputs

Legumes can fix atmospheric nitrogen in symbiosis with compatible bacteria, contributing nitrogen to the system.
p: Agriculture A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Why is matching tractor power to an implement important?
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** It improves field efficiency and reduces unnecessary fuel use and machine stress

Correct matching improves power utilisation, work rate, fuel efficiency and machine longevity.
p: Agriculture A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Which market function adds value by making produce more uniform in quality and presentation before sale?
a: Grading and standardisation classify produce according to defined quality characteristics, supporting market transactions.
p: Agriculture A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: If an enterprise has gross income of $24,000 and variable costs of $14,500, what is its gross margin?
p: Agriculture A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Which soil-management practice most directly improves infiltration while reducing erosion and preserving surface residue?
a:
**Correct Answer (B):** Conservation/minimum tillage

Reduced disturbance and residue retention protect the surface and can improve infiltration and soil structure.
p: Agriculture A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Which climatic variable is especially useful when estimating evaporative demand of a crop?
a:
**Correct Answer (C):** Temperature and atmospheric humidity

Temperature and humidity strongly influence atmospheric evaporative demand; wind and radiation are also important.
p: Agriculture A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: Which feature of a well-designed agricultural experiment most directly improves the ability to separate treatment effects from random variation?
a:
**Correct Answer (D):** Replication and randomisation

Replication estimates experimental variation while randomisation reduces systematic allocation bias.
p: Agriculture A-Level Paper 1 — Multiple Choice

q: What does a soil's Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC) measure?
a:
**Correct Answer (A):** Ability of negatively charged clay and humus colloids to hold and exchange basic cations (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺)

High humus and 2:1 clay (montmorillonite) increase CEC, boosting nutrient retention against leaching.
