q: Alexander Kanengoni — *Echoing Silences*: Discuss how Munashe's wartime haunting by a murdered mother and baby exposes unhealed spiritual and psychological wounds left by the liberation war. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Trauma & Traditional Cleansing:** Western psychiatric isolation fails until traditional ngozi/chikaranga reckoning confronts silenced atrocities amidst post-war political betrayal [25 marks].
p: Literature in English A-Level Paper 2 — Zimbabwean Literature

q: Nadine Gordimer — *July's People*: Evaluate how inverting master-servant power when Maureen and Bam Smales flee Johannesburg to July's rural village exposes the illusions of white South African liberalism. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Collapse of Liberal Paternalism:** Without keys, car, gun, and urban privilege, Maureen cannot recognise July's authentic humanity—exposing language as site of power [25 marks].
p: Literature in English A-Level Paper 2 — Zimbabwean Literature

q: Freedom Nyamubaya / Samuel Chimsoro — Zimbabwean Liberation Poetry: Compare how post-independence Zimbabwean poets celebrate guerrilla sacrifice while questioning unfulfilled promises of independence. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Critical Patriotism:** Vivid battle imagery, contrast between fallen comrades in unmarked graves and comfortable elites, insisting true freedom demands ongoing social justice [25 marks].
p: Literature in English A-Level Paper 2 — Zimbabwean Literature

q: Meja Mwangi — *Kill Me Quick*: Analyse how urban slums ("Shanty Land") and youth unemployment trap Meja and Maina in Nairobi despite high school education. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Urban Alienation:** Graphic depiction of garbage-bin survival, quarry exploitation, and broken hopes of rural parents awaiting remittances critiques neocolonial class neglect [25 marks].
p: Literature in English A-Level Paper 2 — Zimbabwean Literature

q: Language Debate in African Literature (Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o vs Chinua Achebe): Evaluate whether writing in English can authentically express Zimbabwean and African experience or perpetuates cultural alienation. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Ngũgĩ (*Decolonising the Mind*):** Language carries culture/memory; indigenous tongues (Gikuyu, ChiShona, IsiNdebele) reach working peasants directly [12 marks].
- **Achebe & Zimbabwean Bilingual Synthesis:** Re-forging English with African proverbs/idioms (Hove, Dangarembga) reaches Pan-African readerships, while vernacular publishing must expand simultaneously [13 marks].
p: Literature in English A-Level Paper 2 — Zimbabwean Literature

q: Okot p'Bitek — *Song of Lawino* & *Song of Ocol*: Discuss how Lawino's satirical Acholi praise-lament defends indigenous dignity against Ocol's self-hating colonial mimicry. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Voice & Metaphor:** Earthy pumpkin proverb ("Let no one uproot the pumpkin in the old homestead"), mockery of Tina's bleached skin/wigs, exposing spiritual emptiness behind Ocol's imported political slogans [25 marks].
p: Literature in English A-Level Paper 2 — Zimbabwean Literature

q: Comparative Zimbabwean Essay: Discuss how two Zimbabwean writers portray the impact of colonialism or war on the integrity of the traditional family unit. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Comparative Depth:** E.g., *Nervous Conditions* (educational estrangement/patriarchy) alongside *Waiting for the Rain* or *Harvest of Thorns*—weighing economic migration, mission schools, and generational trauma rigorously [25 marks].
p: Literature in English A-Level Paper 2 — Zimbabwean Literature

q: Compare a Flashy Storm Hydrograph with a Subdued (Attenuated) Storm Hydrograph in a drainage basin and explain four physical and human basin factors controlling lag time and peak discharge. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Hydrograph Contrast:** Flashy shows short lag time, steep rising limb, high peak discharge; Subdued shows long lag time, gentle rising limb, broad low peak [7 marks].
- **Controlling Factors:** (1) Permeability/rock type (granite/clay boosts overland flow vs porous sandstone percolation); (2) Rainfall intensity vs infiltration capacity (Hortonian overland flow); (3) Basin shape & slope (circular steep basins concentrate flow fast); (4) Land use (urban tarmac/deforestation lowers interception vs dense savanna woodland) [18 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Explain the Hjulström Curve relationship between river velocity and sediment particle size for erosion, transportation, and deposition, highlighting the anomalous behaviour of clay and silt. [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Curves:** Critical erosion velocity vs settling/deposition velocity against log particle size (0.001 mm – 100 mm) [5 marks].
- **Sand vs Clay Anomaly:** Medium sand (0.1–1 mm) erodes at lowest velocity (~20 cm/s); finer clay/silt particles require unexpectedly HIGH erosion velocities due to strong electrochemical cohesion and smooth bed surface [6 marks]. Once suspended, clay stays transported down to near-zero velocities [4 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Describe the Tricellular Model of global atmospheric circulation (Hadley, Ferrel, and Polar cells) and explain how seasonal shifts of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) drive Zimbabwe's wet and dry seasons. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Tricellular Model:** Thermal Hadley ascent at equator (0°), subtropical descent (~30° N/S creating Kalahari/Sahara arid belts), Ferrel mid-latitude westerlies, Polar easterlies + Coriolis deflection [13 marks].
- **ITCZ over Zimbabwe:** In austral summer (Nov–Mar), overhead sun shifts south to Tropic of Capricorn, drawing warm moist Congo Air and NE/SE trade convergence over Zimbabwe (convectional rain). In winter (May–Aug), Botswana/Subtropical High dominance brings dry stable descending air [12 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Explain the formation, vertical structure, and destructive hazards of Tropical Cyclones (e.g., Cyclone Idai, March 2019), and assess how their intensity dissipates inland over eastern Zimbabwe. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Formation:** Sea surface temperatures ≥ 26.5°C, Coriolis force (≥ 5° from equator), low wind shear, latent heat release fueling deep cumulonimbus eyewall around calm subsiding eye [10 marks].
- **Inland Impact & Decay:** Orographic uplift against Chimanimani/Eastern Highlands triggers catastrophic rainfall, landslides, and flash floods before loss of warm ocean moisture and surface friction weaken the storm [10 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Explain how El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events alter Walker Circulation over the Pacific and trigger severe agricultural droughts across Southern Africa. [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Normal vs El Niño Walker Cell:** Trade winds weaken/reverse; warm sea surface anomalies shift to central/eastern Pacific, displacing convective ascent eastward [8 marks].
- **Zimbabwe Impact:** Teleconnections strengthen high-pressure subsidence over Southern Africa during peak summer (Dec–Feb), suppressing ITCZ cloud bands and causing mid-season dry spells and crop failure [7 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: With reference to Peltier's weathering diagram, analyse how temperature and precipitation regimes govern chemical versus physical weathering, with specific reference to granite bornhardts (dwalas) and tors in Zimbabwe. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Climate Controls (Peltier):** Chemical weathering (hydrolysis, carbonation, oxidation) dominates in hot, humid climates (doubles rate per +10°C—van't Hoff); physical freeze-thaw/insolation dominates in cold or arid regimes [8 marks].
- **Zimbabwe Granite Landforms (Matobo/Domboshava):** Deep subsurface chemical etching along rectangular joints during humid Tertiary phases followed by stripping of regolith (exhumation/pressure-release sheeting) exposes dome-shaped bornhardts and joint-controlled castle kopjes/tors [12 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Outline Plate Tectonics theory and compare the landforms and hazards produced at Constructive, Destructive (Subduction), and Collision margins, referencing the East African Rift Valley. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Mechanisms:** Slab pull, ridge push, mantle convection driving lithospheric plates [5 marks].
- **Margins:** Constructive (Mid-Atlantic Ridge / East African Rift horst & graben normal faults, basaltic volcanism); Destructive (ocean trench, Benioff-zone explosive andesitic volcanoes, tsunamis); Collision (Himalayan fold mountains, shallow high-magnitude quakes) [15 marks].
- **East African Rift:** Divergent continental rifting with Lake Tanganyika/Malawi grabens and shield/stratovolcanoes [5 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Compare Wood's (1942) four-element Slope Profile Model with Young's/King's Pediplanation theory in tropical savanna landscapes. [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Four Slope Elements:** Waxing/convex summit (soil creep), Free face/rock cliff (rockfall/joint control), Constant/debris slope (angle of repose), Waning concave pediment (sheetwash) [8 marks].
- **King's Pediplanation:** Parallel scarp retreat maintains constant steep free-face angle leaving expanding gently concave pediments coalescing into a pediplain dotted with residual inselbergs [7 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Explain the Gersmehl Nutrient Cycle model and contrast nutrient store sizes and transfer rates between a Tropical Rainforest and a Tropical Savanna (Miombo Woodland) ecosystem. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Gersmehl Stores & Flows:** Biomass, Litter, Soil stores linked by uptake, fallout, decomposition, leaching, weathering [8 marks].
- **Comparison:** Tropical Rainforest holds huge Biomass store with rapid decomposition & intense leaching (thin ferralsols). Miombo Savanna holds much smaller Biomass, larger relative Litter/Soil nutrient retention during dry season, and regular fire mineral-ash recycling [12 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Define a Soil Catena and explain how topography and drainage create predictable soil property sequences down a Zimbabwean granitic slope (from crest to vlei/dambo). [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Crest/Upper Slope:** Eluviation, thin coarse sandy well-drained red/brown fersiallitic soils [5 marks].
- **Mid-Slope:** Throughflow moves bases & clay downslope; thicker loam profiles [5 marks].
- **Lower Vlei/Dambo:** Illuviation accumulates fine dark vertisol/hydromorphic clay (gleying, anaerobic iron reduction mottling) with high seasonal water table [5 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Distinguish between River Braiding and River Meandering in alluvial channels, explaining the flow hydraulics (helicoidal flow, thalweg) behind pools, riffles, and point bars. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Braided Channels:** High seasonal sediment load, easily erodible banks, and fluctuating discharge split flow around shifting eyot gravel/sand bars [8 marks].
- **Meanders & Hydraulics:** Pool-and-riffle sequences initiate sinuous thalweg; centrifugal pressure sets up secondary helicoidal corkscrew currents eroding outer river cliffs and depositing sorted inner point bars [12 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Explain how karst limestone landscapes (such as Chinhoyi Caves) develop through carbonation weathering and fluctuating phreatic water tables. [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Carbonation Chemistry:** Rainwater absorbs CO₂ forming weak carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), dissolving insoluble CaCO₃ into soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate Ca(HCO₃)₂ along bedding planes and vertical joints [8 marks].
- **Landforms:** Limestone pavements, dolines, sinkholes, subterranean caverns below the water table later drained by base-level lowering, and speleothems (stalactites/stalagmites) [7 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Assess the physical causes of Coastal Erosion and Deposition, explaining the formation of a headland-and-bay sequence, wave-cut platform, and spit. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Erosion Processes:** Hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition, solution + wave refraction concentrating energy on resistant headlands [8 marks].
- **Landforms:** Cliff recession leaves intertidal wave-cut platform; longshore drift transports sediment past coastline bends forming hooked sand spits and salt-marsh lagoons behind them [12 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Explain atmospheric stability, instability, and conditional instability using Environmental Lapse Rate (ELR), Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate (DALR), and Saturated Adiabatic Lapse Rate (SALR). [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Rates:** DALR (~9.8°C/km) for unsaturated rising parcels; SALR (~5–6°C/km) above lifting condensation level due to latent heat release [5 marks].
- **Cases:** Absolute stability (ELR < SALR: resists uplift, stratus/fog/inversions); Absolute instability (ELR > DALR: buoyant towering cumulonimbus storms); Conditional instability (SALR < ELR < DALR) [10 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Evaluate the role of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and Satellite Remote Sensing (NDVI, thermal bands) in monitoring drought, deforestation, and flood hazards in Zimbabwe. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Remote Sensing Capabilities:** Multi-spectral NDVI tracks seasonal vegetation stress/famine early warning; radar/SAR penetrates cloud cover to map Zambezi/Save flood extents; Landsat time-series quantify woodland clearing [10 marks].
- **GIS Integration & Limits:** Overlays elevation DEMs, population density, and road access to target emergency aid; constrained by cloud cover in optical sensors, high-res licensing costs, and ground-truthing needs [10 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Contrast Urban Heat Island (UHI) microclimates with surrounding rural areas and explain how urban design alters wind, precipitation, and air quality. [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Causes of UHI:** Low albedo dark asphalt/roofs, high thermal capacity brick/concrete, lack of evapotranspiration vegetation, anthropogenic vehicle/AC waste heat [8 marks].
- **Effects:** 2–5°C warmer nocturnal minima, enhanced afternoon convection/downwind storms, canyon street gusts vs overall friction slowdown, photochemical smog inversions [7 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Explain Plagioclimax and Secondary Succession in ecosystems, using Zimbabwean fire-climax savanna grasslands and abandoned farmland as examples. [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Secondary Succession:** Recolonisation of disturbed land retaining soil/seedbank (pioneer grasses → shrubs → acacia/miombo canopy) [7 marks].
- **Plagioclimax:** Ecosystem arrested from reaching climatic climax by repeated human/biotic disturbance such as annual dry-season burning, grazing, or woodcutting, favouring fire-resistant grasses and thick-barked trees [8 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Assess the physical causes of Mass Movement (rotational slumping, mudflows, rockfalls) and evaluate two slope-stabilisation engineering measures. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Shear Stress vs Shear Strength:** Heavy rainfall adds pore-water pressure reducing friction, undercutting toes by rivers/roads increases slope angle, seismic shocks/deforestation remove root cohesion [10 marks].
- **Engineering Measures:** Weep-hole sub-surface drainage pipes (reduce pore pressure), rock bolts/gabion retaining walls/shotcrete/terrace grading—evaluate high cost vs effectiveness on Chimanimani mountain highways [10 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Explain Darcy's Law and distinguish between Confined and Unconfined Aquifers, assessing threats to groundwater sustainability around Harare and Chitungwiza. [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Aquifers:** Unconfined receives direct surface recharge; confined lies trapped beneath impermeable aquiclude creating artesian pressure; Darcy's Law Q = K·A·(dh/dl) [7 marks].
- **Threats:** Uncontrolled urban borehole drilling causing cone-of-depression drawdown, paved surfaces blocking recharge, pit-latrine/industrial leachate contamination [8 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Evaluate the natural versus anthropogenic drivers of Pleistocene Glacial/Interglacial cycles (Milankovitch orbital forcing) compared with modern Enhanced Greenhouse Global Warming. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Natural Drivers:** Eccentricity (100 kyr), Axial Tilt/Obliquity (41 kyr), Precession (23 kyr), solar variation, volcanic aerosols [8 marks].
- **Anthropogenic Drivers & Evaluation:** Rapid post-industrial rise in CO₂ (>420 ppm), CH₄, and N₂O outpaces natural orbital timescales by orders of magnitude, amplifying positive albedo and permafrost feedbacks [12 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Explain how Soil Erosion (splash, sheet, rill, and gully erosion) occurs on communal arable slopes and evaluate biological versus mechanical conservation methods. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Mechanisms:** Raindrop detachment (splash) on bare crusted soil → overland sheet flow → concentrated rills → incised headward-advancing dongas/gullies [8 marks].
- **Conservation:** Mechanical (contour ridges, storm drains, gabion check-dams) vs Biological (vetiver grass strips, zero-tillage mulching, agroforestry cover crops) [12 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Compare Aeolian landforms in hot arid deserts (barchans, seif dunes, yardangs, zeugen) and explain the processes of deflation, saltation, and abrasion. [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Wind Processes:** Deflation hollows out fine dust leaving desert lag pavement; Saltation bounces sand <1.5 m causing basal sandblasting abrasion on mushroom pedestals [7 marks].
- **Landforms:** Crescentic barchans (unidirectional wind, limited sand) vs long linear seif dunes (bimodal winds); streamlined yardangs vs caprock zeugen [8 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Explain the Water Balance Equation (P = Q + E ± ΔS) and show how seasonal soil moisture budget graphs identify periods of soil moisture surplus, utilisation, deficit, and recharge. [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Equation:** Precipitation = Runoff + Evapotranspiration ± Soil/Groundwater Storage change [5 marks].
- **Four Phases:** When P > PE (rainy season) soil recharges to field capacity then generates runoff surplus; when PE > P (dry season) plants utilise stored moisture until deficit limits growth [10 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Evaluate the effectiveness of Early Warning Systems, Floodplain Zoning, and Dam Reservoirs (e.g., Tokwe-Mukosi / Kariba) in mitigating fluvial flood hazards. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Hard Engineering (Dams/Levees):** Controls downstream peak flows and generates hydro/irrigation, though expensive, traps silt, and creates catastrophic dam-breach risk if overwhelmed [9 marks].
- **Soft Management (Zoning & Forecasts):** Keeps high-value assets off floodplains and saves lives via early SMS evacuation alerts, though informal settlement enforcement is hard [11 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Using Spearman's Rank Correlation or Chi-Square concepts in Physical Geography fieldwork, explain how a student tests whether river pebble roundness increases significantly with distance downstream. [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Sampling & Measurement:** Systematic downstream sample sites (10+ sites); random/stratified selection of 20–30 pebbles/site measured on Powers Roundness Scale + Cailleux index [6 marks].
- **Statistical Test (Spearman's rₛ):** Rank distance (x) and mean roundness (y), compute rₛ = 1 − [6Σd² / (n³−n)], compare against critical values at p=0.05/0.01 to accept/reject H₀, noting lithological/tributary caveats [9 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 1 — Physical Geography

q: Compare Malthusian and Boserupian theories regarding the relationship between population growth and food supply, evaluating which better explains modern agricultural trends in sub-Saharan Africa. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Malthus (1798):** Geometric population growth outstrips arithmetic food growth, triggering preventive (moral restraint) and positive checks (famine, war, disease) [8 marks].
- **Boserup (1965):** Rising population density acts as catalyst driving agricultural intensification (shortened fallow, irrigation, green-revolution hybrids, mechanisation) [9 marks].
- **Evaluation:** Boserup explains global yield surges where capital/extension exist, but localized Malthusian vulnerability persists under climate droughts, soil exhaustion, and weak rural infrastructure [8 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Analyse the five-stage Demographic Transition Model (DTM) and evaluate its applicability to the changing birth rates, death rates, and age pyramids of Zimbabwe and SADC nations. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **DTM Stages 1–5:** High stationary → Early expanding → Late expanding → Low stationary → Declining [8 marks].
- **Zimbabwe Application & Critique:** Zimbabwe reflects late Stage 2 / Stage 3 with falling fertility via female education and contraception alongside death rate fluctuations from HIV/AIDS impacts (now stabilising via ART), showing the Western Eurocentric model needs adaptation for health shocks and migration [12 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Explain Von Thünen's Agricultural Location Model, stating its simplifying assumptions and assessing why modern refrigeration, highways, and command policies distort its concentric land-use zones around Harare. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Model & Bid Rent:** Locational rent R = Y(P−C) − Y·t·d places perishable/high-transport-cost horticulture & dairying closest to the central market, then forestry, arable grains, and extensive ranching furthest out [10 marks].
- **Real-world Distortions:** Refrigerated trucks, multiple urban markets, fertile soil anisotropy, irrigation dams, and government pricing/land tenure distort ideal rings [10 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Evaluate Alfred Weber's Least-Cost Industrial Location Theory, distinguishing between weight-losing and weight-gaining industries with Zimbabwean manufacturing examples. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Weber Model:** Minimises transport cost (Locational Triangle of Material Index MI), labour cost, and agglomeration economies [8 marks].
- **Examples:** Weight-losing (MI > 1: iron smelting at Redcliff/Kwekwe, sugar milling in Lowveld, cement near limestone) locates at raw materials; Weight-gaining (MI < 1: soft-drink bottling, bakeries) locates at urban markets; evaluate neglect of tariffs, electricity availability, and environmental zoning [12 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Using Christaller's Central Place Theory (Threshold Population and Range of a Good), explain the hierarchy of urban settlements in Zimbabwe from rural growth points to Harare. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Concepts:** Range = max distance consumers travel; Threshold = min population/demand needed to sustain a service; Hexagonal non-overlapping service hinterlands (k=3,4,7) [9 marks].
- **Hierarchy:** Low-order rural service centres (groceries, primary clinic — small range/threshold) → District growth points/towns (bank, secondary hospital) → Bulawayo/Harare high-order regional cities (universities, specialist surgery, airports) [11 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Compare the concentric zone (Burgess), sector (Hoyt), and multiple-nuclei (Harris & Ullman) urban land-use models and evaluate how colonial planning shaped Harare's dual urban morphology. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Classic Models:** Burgess rings, Hoyt transport wedges, Harris & Ullman polycentric hubs [10 marks].
- **Harare Morphology:** Historical segregation placed low-density affluent suburbs (Borrowdale/Mount Pleasant) in well-drained northern sectors and high-density industrial-worker townships (Mbare, Highfield, Chitungwiza satellite) in southern/south-western sectors alongside industrial rail corridors—now modified by CBD edge office parks and peri-urban growth [15 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Assess the causes, socioeconomic contributions, and environmental/planning challenges of the Informal Sector in African cities. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Drivers:** Formal job contraction, rapid urban migration, low entry capital barriers [5 marks].
- **Contributions vs Challenges:** Provides livelihoods, cheap urban goods/recycling, and entrepreneurial incubators (Siya So / Magaba), yet creates congestion, unserviced sanitation waste, tax base erosion, and precarious worker safety [15 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: With reference to Lee's Push-Pull Migration Model and Ravenstein's Laws, analyse the impacts of skilled international emigration ("brain drain") on Zimbabwe versus the role of diaspora remittances. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Push/Pull/Intervening Obstacles:** Economic opportunities & wage differentials pull nurses, engineers, and teachers abroad despite visa costs [8 marks].
- **Impacts:** Loss of public-funded human capital and strained clinics/schools vs substantial forex remittances sustaining household consumption, housing, and education fees [17 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Evaluate the causes and possible remedies for Urban Traffic Congestion in major cities such as Harare and Bulawayo. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Causes:** Dominance of private vehicles & low-capacity kombis, radial CBD concentration, uncoordinated traffic signals, absence of suburban light rail, peak commuter waves from Chitungwiza/Norton [8 marks].
- **Solutions:** High-capacity Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) / commuter rail corridors, park-and-ride hubs, outer ring-roads, decongesting offices to suburban nodes, congestion charging—evaluate funding & enforcement hurdles [12 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Explain the "Resource Curse" hypothesis and assess how Mineral Beneficiation and Value Addition policies can transform Zimbabwe's mining sector (platinum, lithium, gold). [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Resource Curse:** Over-reliance on raw ore exports fuels price vulnerability, Dutch disease, weak linkages, and rent-seeking [7 marks].
- **Beneficiation:** Refining concentrates, manufacturing battery-grade lithium salts or platinum catalysts captures higher export value, builds engineering skills, and creates multiplier factories—constrained by reliable high-voltage power supply and refining capex [13 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Compare Rostow's Five Stages of Economic Growth with Friedmann's Core-Periphery Model in explaining regional development disparities within Zimbabwe. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Rostow:** Linear domestic stages (Traditional → Preconditions → Take-off → Maturity → Mass Consumption) criticised for ignoring colonial trade structures and external debt [10 marks].
- **Friedmann Core-Periphery:** Cumulative causation concentrates industry, talent, and investment in core hubs (Harare-Bulawayo rail spine) leaving peripheral rural districts lagging via backwash effects unless deliberate spread/decentralisation growth points intervene [15 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Evaluate the environmental, economic, and social impacts of Large-Scale Hydroelectric Dams (e.g., Kariba Dam) versus Distributed Solar Mini-Grids for rural energy security. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Large Hydro:** High baseload capacity and multi-purpose irrigation/fisheries, yet suffers severe El Niño drought vulnerability, community displacement, and huge grid transmission losses to remote villages [10 marks].
- **Solar Mini-Grids:** Fast modular deployment, zero transmission loss, climate-resilient, empowers rural clinics/cold-chains, though battery storage costs limit heavy industrial smelting [10 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Explain the principles and stages of an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) under Zimbabwe's Environmental Management Agency (EMA) before approving a major open-cast mine or highway. [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Purpose:** Precautionary decision tool weighing biophysical and socioeconomic impacts prior to project approval [4 marks].
- **Stages:** Screening → Scoping & Baseline Survey → Public Stakeholder Consultation → Impact Prediction & Mitigation Design (EMS) → EMA Review Decision → Post-implementation Auditing & Decommissioning bonds [11 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Assess the opportunities and challenges of Sustainable Ecotourism (including CAMPFIRE community conservation programmes) for rural livelihoods in Zimbabwe. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Mechanism:** Devolves wildlife benefits (photographic & safari revenues) to rural wards so communities value conservation over poaching [8 marks].
- **Evaluation:** Builds local clinics/schools and tolerates human-wildlife conflict when revenues reach households transparently; vulnerable to global travel shocks, governance leakage, and drought [12 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Explain the Globalisation drivers (containerisation, TNCs, ICT) and evaluate why benefits of global trade have been distributed unevenly between core and developing economies. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Drivers:** Falling transport/communication costs, trade liberalisation, Transnational Corporations dispersing assembly globally [8 marks].
- **Uneven Distribution:** Value capture concentrates in R&D/brand hubs in core countries while developing nations face tariff escalation on processed exports, commodity price volatility, and infrastructure deficits [12 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Contrast Urban Renewal (Gentrification & Redevelopment) with Slum Upgrading ("Sites and Services") as strategies for improving low-income urban housing. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Demolition/Redevelopment:** Replaces dilapidated stock with modern apartments, but displaces poor residents to unserviced fringes and destroys social networks [9 marks].
- **In-situ Upgrading / Sites-and-Services:** Provides secure land tenure, piped water, sewerage, and incremental self-build plots—retains community cohesion and matches household budgets when paired with micro-mortgages [11 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Analyse the causes of Food Insecurity in semi-arid Regions IV and V of Zimbabwe and evaluate drought-resilient farming innovations (Pfumvudza/Intwasa, small grains, solar drip irrigation). [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Causes:** Erratic rainfall, dry spells, sandy nutrient-poor soils, post-harvest weevil losses, input price barriers [7 marks].
- **Remedies:** Conservation basins + mulching trap scarce moisture & organic fertility; drought-tolerant sorghum/millet/pearl millet outperform maize in dry years; small solar drip schemes boost winter nutrition [13 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Using Burgess/Bid-Rent curves, explain why commercial retail and finance concentrate at the Peak Land Value Intersection (CBD) and why "Out-of-Town" retail parks are expanding. [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Bid-Rent:** Finance and flagship retail require maximum pedestrian accessibility and can outbid industry/housing per m² in the CBD core [8 marks].
- **Suburban Decentralisation:** Rising CBD congestion, parking scarcity, and high land rates push supermarkets and offices to accessible suburban hubs (e.g., Borrowdale/Msasa/Westgate) [7 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Distinguish between Renewable and Non-Renewable Energy transitions and evaluate the socio-economic barriers slowing adoption of clean cooking alternatives over fuelwood in rural areas. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Fuelwood Reliance:** ~60%+ rural energy uses wood/charcoal, driving deforestation around towns and indoor smoke respiratory illness [8 marks].
- **Barriers:** Upfront cost of LPG cylinders/stoves/biogas digesters, unreliable rural gas refilling networks, free collection of deadwood, cultural cooking preferences [12 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Evaluate the role of Transport Networks (Kansky's Beta & Gamma network connectivity indices, Beira/North-South corridors) in unlocking landlocked Zimbabwe's trade competitiveness. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Indices & Corridors:** Higher Beta (e/v) and Gamma indices measure network efficiency/redundancy; corridors linking Beitbridge, Forbes-Beira, and Chirundu connect inland mines/farms to sea ports [10 marks].
- **Evaluation:** Upgraded NRZ rail freight and one-stop border posts (Chirundu/Beitbridge) sharply lower bulk transit costs compared with overloaded haulage trucks damaging highways [10 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Explain how Population Pyramids reflect Dependency Ratios and future planning needs for Education, Healthcare, and Pensions across contrasting countries. [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Youthful Pyramid (Zimbabwe):** Wide base → high youth dependency ratio, urgent need for schools, maternal/paediatric health, and rapid formal job creation [8 marks].
- **Ageing Pyramid (Japan/UK):** Narrow base, broad apex → rising old-age dependency, pension funding strain, geriatric care, and labour automation needs [7 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Compare Spatial Allocation of Health Services and Water Supply between urban and rural districts, assessing the role of devolution in narrowing spatial inequality. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Disparities:** Urban centres concentrate referral hospitals, specialists, and piped supply; remote rural wards face long travel distances, seasonal boreholes, and referral delays [10 marks].
- **Devolution Assessment:** Directing fiscal grants to Rural District Councils targets local clinic and borehole priorities better if coupled with transparent audit capacity [10 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Evaluate how Agglomeration Economies and Industrial Inertia keep established manufacturing clusters (e.g., Workington/Msasa/Belmont) thriving even after original locational advantages change. [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Internal & External Economies:** Shared skilled labour pool, component suppliers, utilities, repair services, and lower freight interchange costs [9 marks].
- **Inertia vs Diseconomies:** Sunk factory capital keeps firms anchored until traffic congestion, high municipal rates, and ageing infrastructure push decentralisation to outlying industrial parks [6 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Assess the socio-economic and environmental trade-offs of Rapid Peri-Urban Residential Sprawl on Harare's wetlands and agricultural greenbelt. [20 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [20 marks]
- **Pressures:** Housing backlog pushes unregulated subdivisions onto seasonal vlei wetlands and former market-gardening farms [7 marks].
- **Impacts & Policy:** Destroys natural flood sponges and Lake Chivero water filtration, increases cholera/borehole contamination risks, and lengthens commuter infrastructure costs; requires compact high-density infill and strict EMA wetland enforcement [13 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: Explain how a geographer uses Nearest Neighbour Analysis (Rₙ) to objectively classify rural settlement patterns (nucleated, random, or uniform/dispersed). [15 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [15 marks]
- **Formula:** Rₙ = 2 · d̄_obs · √(n / A), where d̄_obs = mean distance to nearest neighbour, n = settlements, A = study area [6 marks].
- **Scale Interpretation:** Rₙ = 0 (completely clustered/nucleated—floodplain or borehole clusters); Rₙ = 1.0 (random); Rₙ ≈ 2.15 (uniform dispersed hexagonal spacing—regular smallholdings) [9 marks].
p: Geography A-Level Paper 2 — Human Geography

q: 'Economic factors were more important than political factors in explaining the Scramble for and Partition of Africa.' Discuss.
a:
Economic: search for raw materials and new markets following the Industrial Revolution; control of strategic trade routes/resources (Suez, Congo basin, Southern African gold/diamonds); speculative chartered-company capital (e.g. BSAC in Rhodesia).
Political/strategic: inter-European rivalry and prestige (Anglo-French/Anglo-German competition); the Berlin Conference (1884-85) formalising and accelerating claims; strategic protection of existing possessions (Cape to Cairo, Suez route to India).
Other factors: missionary/"civilising mission" ideology and Social Darwinist racial ideology provided justification and practical groundwork.
Mark scheme guidance: reference to historiographical schools (Hobson/Lenin economic-imperialism theory versus Robinson and Gallagher's "official mind"/strategic thesis) expected for top bands, with an independent, evidenced conclusion.
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Assess the reasons for the failure of the First Chimurenga/Umvukela (1896-97) to remove settler rule in Southern Rhodesia.
a:
Military imbalance (Maxim guns, dynamite versus spears/older firearms); incomplete unity across all regions despite notable Shona-Ndebele cooperation (Ranger's historiographical analysis of religious coordination); separate Ndebele peace negotiated at the Matobo indabas (1896) while fighting continued in Mashonaland; British reinforcements following resolution of the Jameson Raid crisis; loss of key leaders (Nehanda, Kaguvi executed 1898). Long-term significance despite military defeat: symbolic legacy invoked in the Second Chimurenga.
Mark scheme guidance: engage explicitly with historiographical debate on the extent of Shona-Ndebele coordination, not mere narration.
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: 'The Land Apportionment Act of 1930 was the single most significant piece of colonial legislation in shaping Zimbabwe's twentieth-century history.' How far do you agree?
a:
Supporting: entrenched racial land segregation with consequences for productivity, migration, and rural poverty across decades; structurally shaped the labour market; fed directly into nationalist grievances, Lancaster House's land clause, and the Fast Track Land Reform Programme from 2000 - a direct causal chain.
Counter-arguments: other legislation was also highly significant (Industrial Conciliation Act 1934; Native Registration Act/pass laws; UDI 1965, precipitating the armed struggle); broader global forces (decolonisation trends, Cold War dynamics, individual leadership) also shaped the century independently of land policy.
Mark scheme guidance: reasoned judgement required; no credit at the top band for a one-sided answer considering no alternative.
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Examine the impact of the Second Chimurenga (liberation war, c.1966-1979) on rural populations in Rhodesia.
a:
Protected/"keep" villages disrupted agriculture, family life and settlement patterns under counter-insurgency logic; rural populations faced violence/coercion from both security forces and, in some cases, guerrilla enforcement against suspected informers; disrupted schooling/health/farming near the Mozambique/Zambia borders; mobilisation of rural civilians as active guerrilla support base (mujibas, chimbwidos) rather than only passive victims; role of spirit mediums in legitimising rural war effort (historiographical debate following Ranger); long-term social change in gender/generational authority structures.
Mark scheme guidance: move beyond a simple "war caused suffering" narrative to analyse rural populations' active and varied roles, with awareness of relevant historiography.
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Explain the nature of political organisation in the Mutapa State and assess the reasons for its long-term decline.
a:
Political organisation: centralised kingship (Mwenemutapa) under Nyatsimba Mutota's dynasty, supported by provincial governors and a tribute system; religious legitimation through ritual/ancestral association; economic base in gold and long-distance trade.
Decline: succession disputes weakening central authority; Portuguese interference in succession (supporting rival claimants) and the destabilising prazo estate system from the sixteenth-seventeenth centuries; competition and eventual displacement of plateau dominance by the rising Rozvi State under Changamire Dombo, who successfully expelled Portuguese influence from the interior.
Mark scheme guidance: candidates should weigh internal (succession) versus external (Portuguese interference, Rozvi rivalry) causes of decline for a balanced top-band answer.
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Compare the nature of British South Africa Company rule (1890-1923) with Responsible Government (1923-1953) in Southern Rhodesia.
a:
BSAC period: combined commercial and governmental functions under Royal Charter; Company-appointed Administrator and Native Commissioners; policy driven substantially by shareholder profit motives (land, mining concessions); marked by forced labour and land alienation provoking the First Chimurenga.
Responsible Government period: locally elected white-minority parliament under the British Crown (from the 1923 referendum), removing direct Company commercial control but continuing and intensifying racially discriminatory land and labour policy (e.g. Land Apportionment Act 1930, Industrial Conciliation Act 1934, Land Husbandry Act 1951).
Mark scheme guidance: candidates should identify genuine continuities (racial land/labour policy) as well as the change in governing structure (Company control removed, settler self-government established) for a full comparative answer.
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Account for the international and Frontline State responses to Ian Smith's Unilateral Declaration of Independence (1965).
a:
Britain and the UN imposed economic sanctions intended to force a negotiated settlement, though enforcement was undermined by sanctions-busting support from apartheid South Africa and Portuguese Mozambique until the mid-1970s.
Frontline States (Zambia, later Mozambique and Tanzania) provided diplomatic condemnation, sanctuary and, over time, crucial military rear-base support to nationalist guerrilla movements, accepting the risk of Rhodesian cross-border retaliation.
The OAU and later the Commonwealth applied continued diplomatic pressure, while the loss of secure Mozambican support after Mozambican independence (1975) significantly increased pressure on the Smith regime by removing a key sanctions-busting and security partner.
Mark scheme guidance: candidates should distinguish the diplomatic/sanctions response from the more materially significant Frontline State military/logistical support, and explain how the balance of pressure shifted over time (especially post-1975).
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: 'The 1963 ZAPU-ZANU split was more about strategy and leadership than ethnicity.' Discuss.
a:
Case for strategy/leadership: disagreement over the pace/method of the struggle (mass mobilisation and eventual armed struggle versus perceived indecisiveness/willingness to negotiate under Nkomo); personal leadership rivalries among senior nationalist figures (Sithole, Mugabe, Nkomo).
Case for ethnic/regional factors: subsequent support bases did develop along partially regional/ethnic lines (ZAPU strongest in Matabeleland, ZANU strongest in Mashonaland), and rival external backers (USSR for ZAPU/ZIPRA, China for ZANU/ZANLA) reinforced organisational separation.
Historians generally caution against a purely ethnic explanation for the initial 1963 split itself, viewing ethnic/regional patterns as having developed and hardened over the following years of separate organisational and military development rather than being the primary original cause.
Mark scheme guidance: candidates should engage critically with both interpretations and reach a supported judgement rather than presenting only one explanation as self-evidently correct.
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Examine the extent to which external (Cold War) support shaped the strategies and outcomes of ZANLA and ZIPRA during the liberation war.
a:
Soviet support to ZAPU/ZIPRA and Chinese support to ZANU/ZANLA provided weapons, training and, in ZANLA's case, exposure to Maoist mass-mobilisation guerrilla doctrine visibly reflected in its rural political-military strategy.
External support sustained prolonged armed struggle beyond what domestic resources alone could support, but candidates should also weigh internal/regional factors of comparable or greater importance: rural mass mobilisation, use of religious/spirit medium legitimation, Frontline State rear-base access, and the diplomatic pressure culminating in Lancaster House.
Mark scheme guidance: this is an "examine the extent" question requiring explicit weighing of external Cold War support against internal/regional factors before a reasoned conclusion.
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Assess the significance of the Lancaster House Constitution (1979) in shaping post-independence Zimbabwe.
a:
Immediate significance: ended the liberation war, enabled internationally supervised 1980 elections and internationally recognised independence.
Longer-term significance: the negotiated land clauses (ten-year moratorium, willing-buyer willing-seller principle) constrained the pace of land redistribution, becoming a persistent source of political tension that fed directly into the Fast Track Land Reform Programme from 2000 once the constitutional constraint had lapsed; reserved white parliamentary seats (for a transitional period) and entrenched property protections shaped early post-independence politics and the pace of broader social/economic transformation.
Mark scheme guidance: candidates should trace specific causal links from named constitutional provisions to later developments (especially land reform) for the highest marks, rather than treating Lancaster House and land reform as unconnected events.
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Assess the economic, political, and religious factors behind the rise and eventual decline of the Great Zimbabwe State (c. 1250–1450). [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Rise:** Control of long-distance Swahili coast gold/ivory trade via Sofala, strategic cattle-herding plateau ecology, iron technology, and unifying Mwari/ancestral royal ideology [12 marks].
- **Decline:** Ecological exhaustion (soil/grazing/firewood depletion for dense urban population), shifting Zambezi valley trade routes northwards, succession disputes, and rise of the Mutapa and Torwa successor states [13 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: "The Portuguese presence in the Zambezi Valley between 1500 and 1700 was essentially destructive to African states and trade." How far do you agree? [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Destructive Thesis:** Prazo feudal land seizures, military interference in Mutapa civil wars (e.g., Mavhura/Kapfura treaties of vassalage), forced curva tribute reversal, and disruptive slave/gold extraction [13 marks].
- **Nuance/Agency:** Mutapa and Changamire Rozvi states actively manipulated Portuguese rivalries, imposed taxes (curva), introduced new American crops (maize/cassava), and Changamire Dombo decisively expelled Portuguese armies from the highveld in 1693–95 [12 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Examine the causes and far-reaching political and demographic consequences of the Mfecane in Southern and Central Africa during the early nineteenth century. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Causes:** Competition for fertile grazing & Delagoa Bay ivory trade, ecological drought/Madlathule famine, military revolution under Dingiswayo, Zwide, and Shaka's Zulu age-regiment amabutho system [10 marks].
- **Consequences:** Birth of defensive centralised kingdoms (Ndebele under Mzilikazi, Gaza under Soshangane, Kololo, Ngoni, Basotho under Moshoeshoe), displacement of weaker polities, and profound reshaping of Rozvi-era Zimbabwe [15 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Evaluate the view that the Rudd Concession (1888) and the Royal Charter of 1889 achieved through deception what Cecil John Rhodes could not initially win by force. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Deception Case:** Verbal promises (Charles Rudd/Helm/Moffat assuring Lobengula "only ten white men to dig one hole" under royal jurisdiction) diverged sharply from the written text granting "complete and exclusive charge over all metals and minerals" [13 marks].
- **Broad Imperial Context:** Lobengula also played diplomatic delaying tactics against Boer (Grobler Treaty) & Portuguese threats, while Britain's Charter backed BSAC military conquest via the 1890 Pioneer Column [12 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Account for the outbreak of the 1893 Anglo-Ndebele War and assess its significance for colonial conquest in Zimbabwe. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Causes:** BSAC failure to find a "Second Rand" in Mashonaland, Rhodes/Jameson desire for Matebele goldfields & cattle, Victoria Incident boundary dispute used as pretext by Jameson [13 marks].
- **Significance:** Collapse of Ndebele military independence, looting of cattle & land allocation under Victoria Agreement, establishment of Order-in-Council 1894, and sowing grievances that erupted in Umvukela/First Chimurenga 1896–97 [12 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Analyse the role played by spirit mediums (such as Mbuya Nehanda, Sekuru Kaguvi, and Mlimo) in mobilising and sustaining the 1896–97 First Chimurenga/Umvukela. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Mobilisation & Unity:** Terraced across fragmented Shona chieftaincies and linked Ndebele Mlimo shrines with Mashonaland resistance, casting colonial taxes, locust plagues, and rinderpest as spiritual pollution [13 marks].
- **Limitations & Critique (Terence Ranger vs Julian Cobbing debate):** Spirit mediums inspired fierce morale and tactical warnings, though historians debate whether coordination was pan-territorial or locally negotiated alongside secular chiefs [12 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Evaluate how colonial labour and land policies (such as Hut Tax, Maize Control Acts, and Native Land Husbandry Act of 1951) reshaped African peasant agriculture between 1900 and 1960. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Peasant Rise & Squeeze (Giovanni Arrighi / Ian Phimister):** Initially African peasants supplied mines successfully, until coercive hut taxes, forced eviction to arid Tribal Trust Lands, and dual maize pricing subsidised white commercial farms and engineered cheap mine/farm wage labour [15 marks].
- **NLHA 1951 Impact:** Destocking & individualised plots alienated rural households, driving support directly into nascent urban & nationalist movements (ANCongress / NDP / ZAPU) [10 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Assess the reasons for the rise and collapse of the Central African Federation (1953–1963). [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Rise:** British desire for a counter-weight to apartheid South Africa, Southern Rhodesian settler ambition to tap Northern Rhodesian Copperbelt revenues, economic economies of scale (Kariba/Railways) [12 marks].
- **Collapse:** Fierce African nationalist opposition ("stupid federation") in Nyasaland (Banda) & Northern Rhodesia (Kaunda), uneven distribution of federal wealth favouring Salisbury/Southern Rhodesia, Monckton Commission & Macmillan's "Wind of Change" [13 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: "Christian missionaries were deliberate agents of European imperialism rather than impartial humanitarians in pre-colonial Zimbabwe." Discuss. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Imperial Agent Thesis:** John Moffat & Charles Helm translated and actively endorsed deceptive treaties (Moffat Treaty, Rudd Concession), wrote approvingly of destroying Ndebele power as obstacle to Gospel, and welcomed BSAC rule [13 marks].
- **Humanitarian Contribution:** Introduced formal literacy, indigenous Bible translation/orthography, western healthcare, and several missionaries later critiqued colonial land/labour abuses (e.g., Arthur Shearly Cripps, John White) [12 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Examine the strengths and weaknesses of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU, 1963–2002) in advancing African decolonisation and continental unity. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Strengths:** OAU Liberation Committee (headquartered in Dar es Salaam) provided vital diplomatic, financial, and training backing to ZANU/ZAPU, FRELIMO, ANC, and SWAPO; championed anti-apartheid sanctions [13 marks].
- **Weaknesses:** Doctrine of "non-interference in internal affairs" sheltered dictatorships, scarce funding, ideological Casablanca vs Monrovia lingering splits, and limited intra-African trade integration [12 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Assess the significance of women's participation (as chimbwidos, combatants, and rural organisers) in the success of Zimbabwe's Second Chimurenga (1966–1979). [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Roles:** Women bore arms in ZANLA and ZIPRA (e.g., Joice Mujuru / Margaret Dongo), sustained intelligence & logistics pipelines as chimbwidos carrying food/ammunition across rural pungwes, and ran refugee camp schools/clinics in Mozambique & Zambia [15 marks].
- **Post-war Trajectory:** Earned wartime political legitimacy and the 1982 Legal Age of Majority Act, though patriarchal cultural barriers later resurfaced [10 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Compare the systems of colonial administration used by Britain (Indirect Rule in Northern Nigeria/Uganda) and France (Assimilation and Association in French West Africa). [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **British Indirect Rule (Lugard):** Governed through existing traditional chiefs/emirs, native treasuries, and customary courts—cheaper and preserved local hierarchy, yet struggled in acephalous societies (e.g., Igbo) via artificial "warrant chiefs" [12 marks].
- **French Assimilation/Association:** Centralised direct command through French commandants de cercle, dividing Africans into subjects (*indigénat*) and a tiny French-educated citizen élite in Senegal's Four Communes, shifting pragmatically to Association [13 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Evaluate the causes and outcomes of the Second Phase (1972–1979) versus the Early Battles (1966 Chinhoyi / 1967–68 Wankie-Sinoia) of the armed liberation struggle in Rhodesia. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **1966–68 Phase:** Conventional cross-border incursions suffered heavy casualties against superior Rhodesian air/armour power due to lack of political mobilisation among rural peasantry [10 marks].
- **1972–79 Protracted Maoist Guerrilla Phase:** FRELIMO's Mozambican liberation opened a 1,200 km eastern border; ZANLA mobilised peasants through *pungwes* & spirit mediums while ZIPRA expanded conventional/urban sabotage from Zambia, exhausting settler manpower and forcing Lancaster House [15 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Account for the longevity of the Rozvi Changamire Empire (c. 1680s–1830s) and assess how internal crises paved the way for Nguni invasions. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Longevity:** Strong military discipline (*mambo* armies), monopoly over gold/ivory trade, religious authority anchored at Mwari cult shrines, and strategic Danangombe/Manyanga stone capitals [13 marks].
- **Decline:** Recurring droughts/famines in the early 1800s, protracted succession rivalries among royal houses weakening central armies, leaving the empire vulnerable to Zwangendaba's Ngoni and Mzilikazi's Ndebele [12 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: Evaluate the social and economic achievements and challenges of post-independence Zimbabwe during its first decade (1980–1990). [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Achievements:** Massive expansion in primary/secondary schools and clinics (immunisation/infant mortality drop), minimum wage laws, smallholder peasant maize/cotton boom backed by AFC credit & GMB depots, reconciliation rhetoric [14 marks].
- **Challenges:** Lancaster House willing-buyer/willing-seller limits slowed land reform, Gukurahundi conflict in Matabeleland/Midlands (resolved by 1987 Unity Accord), growing fiscal deficits and drought pressures paving way for ESAP [11 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 1 — African and Zimbabwean History

q: 'Appeasement was a rational response to the international circumstances of the 1930s, not simply a policy of weakness.' Discuss.
a:
For: economic constraints post-Depression limited rearmament capacity; strong anti-war public sentiment (1935 Peace Ballot); some German demands framed as reversing Versailles injustices; the "buying time" revisionist argument (A.J.P. Taylor and successors).
Against: emboldened Hitler (especially after Munich 1938), contributing directly to further aggression; failed to build credible collective security alternatives, arguably pushing Stalin toward the Nazi-Soviet Pact; orthodox historiography (Churchill's account) frames it as a moral/strategic failure.
Mark scheme guidance: explicit engagement with revisionist versus orthodox historiography expected for top bands, structuring an independent evidenced judgement.
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: To what extent was Stalin responsible for the outbreak of the Cold War by 1948?
a:
For Stalin's responsibility: imposition of communist governments across Eastern Europe violating the spirit of Yalta; pressure on Iran/Turkey and support for Greek communist insurgents prompting the Truman Doctrine; the Berlin Blockade (1948-49) as a direct confrontational act.
Alternative views: orthodox historiography blames Soviet expansionism; revisionists (Williams and successors) point to US economic interests (Marshall Plan) and atomic diplomacy as equally provocative; post-revisionists emphasise mutual misperception and structural great-power rivalry; Stalin's actions can be read defensively as securing a buffer zone against renewed German invasion.
Mark scheme guidance: explicit engagement with orthodox, revisionist and post-revisionist schools required for full marks, not a mere list of Soviet actions.
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Examine the reasons for the successes and limitations of the United Nations in maintaining international peace and security since 1945.
a:
Strengths: near-universal membership from the outset; Security Council empowered for binding collective action; peacekeeping operations developed in practice (post-Suez 1956) with documented successes.
Limitations: permanent-member veto power frequently paralysing action during the Cold War and beyond (e.g. Syria); dependence on member state troops/funding limiting independent enforcement; documented failures (Rwanda 1994, Srebrenica 1995) illustrating limits where major-power political will is absent.
Mark scheme guidance: generalisations must be supported with specific case studies on both sides of the argument for the top band.
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: 'Decolonisation in Africa after 1945 was driven primarily by African nationalism rather than by changes in European policy.' Assess this view.
a:
For nationalism: growth of educated African elites and mass political movements (Nkrumah's CPP, ZAPU/ZANU); direct action including armed struggle (Algeria, Mau Mau, Portuguese colonies, Second Chimurenga) forcing negotiation/withdrawal; Pan-African solidarity via Pan-African Congresses and the OAU.
For European policy change: post-war economic exhaustion reducing capacity/appetite for colonial administration; Cold War dynamics reducing international legitimacy for colonialism and increasing UN pressure; Macmillan's 1960 "Wind of Change" reflecting deliberate strategic recalculation; divergent colonial responses (Britain's negotiated transitions versus Portugal's prolonged wars, ending only after 1974's Carnation Revolution) showing metropole-level politics could be decisive.
Mark scheme guidance: reject simple either/or framing; strongest answers show interaction of both factors across specific case studies before a supported judgement.
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Explain the causes and course of the Russian Revolution of 1917 and assess its significance for twentieth-century world history.
a:
Causes: autocratic Tsarist rule, rural poverty, urban industrial unrest, and the destabilising strain of the First World War.
Course: the February Revolution forced Nicholas II's abdication; the Provisional Government's continuation of the war undermined its support; the Bolsheviks under Lenin seized power in the October Revolution, promising "Peace, Bread, Land," followed by withdrawal from the war (Brest-Litovsk, 1918) and civil war (1918-1921).
Significance: established the world's first communist state, providing an ideological and material model/inspiration for later revolutionary and anti-colonial movements globally (including some African liberation movements), and set up the ideological rivalry that would shape the twentieth-century Cold War.
Mark scheme guidance: candidates should link the Revolution's domestic events to its longer-term global ideological significance for the top band, not describe 1917 in isolation.
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Assess the impact of Stalinism (collectivisation, the Five-Year Plans and the Purges) on the Soviet Union in the 1930s.
a:
Economic impact: rapid, state-directed industrialisation under the Five-Year Plans significantly expanded Soviet heavy industrial capacity, though often at the cost of consumer goods production and with unreliable official statistics.
Agricultural impact: forced collectivisation of agriculture met fierce resistance (notably from kulaks) and contributed to catastrophic famine, most severely in Ukraine (the Holodomor) but affecting other regions, with millions of deaths.
Political impact: the Purges (Great Terror, mid-late 1930s) eliminated real and perceived political rivals within the party, military and wider society through show trials, executions and the Gulag labour camp system, consolidating Stalin's personal dictatorship at immense human cost.
Mark scheme guidance: candidates should weigh genuine industrial/military-capacity gains against the severe human cost for a balanced top-band assessment.
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Explain the rise of Fascism in Italy under Mussolini by 1925 and compare it briefly with Hitler's rise in Germany.
a:
Italy: post-WWI economic disruption, unfulfilled territorial claims ("mutilated victory"), fear of socialist/communist revolution among the middle and upper classes, and weak, unstable liberal governments created conditions Mussolini's Fascists exploited through paramilitary intimidation (Blackshirts) and the March on Rome (1922), after which King Victor Emmanuel III appointed him Prime Minister; Mussolini then used the Acerbo Law and further intimidation to consolidate a one-party dictatorship by 1925.
Comparison with Germany: both rose amid post-war economic disruption and fear of communism, using paramilitary intimidation and eventually legal/constitutional routes to power (Mussolini via royal appointment, Hitler via presidential appointment) before consolidating dictatorial power through further legal and coercive measures.
Mark scheme guidance: candidates should identify at least two genuine points of comparison and, ideally, one point of difference (e.g. differing constitutional mechanisms) for full marks.
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Examine the causes and global consequences of the Great Depression (from 1929).
a:
Causes: speculative US stock market excess ("buying on margin"), agricultural/industrial overproduction outpacing demand, and uneven wealth distribution limiting broad consumer purchasing power, culminating in the 1929 Wall Street Crash and subsequent banking and credit collapse.
Global consequences: international trade collapsed (worsened by protectionist tariffs such as the US Smoot-Hawley Tariff), causing severe hardship in export-dependent economies including colonial territories; political instability in Europe (contributing to Nazi electoral gains in Germany); in the USA, the New Deal provided partial relief and reform, though full recovery is generally linked to Second World War production.
Mark scheme guidance: candidates should trace the Depression's effects beyond the USA to demonstrate genuine global/international consequences for top marks.
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Assess the significance of the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) as a turning point in the Cold War.
a:
Immediate significance: brought the superpowers to the brink of direct nuclear conflict, resolved through negotiation (Soviet missile withdrawal for a US non-invasion pledge and secret removal of US missiles from Turkey).
Longer-term significance: prompted improved crisis-communication mechanisms (the Moscow-Washington hotline) and contributed to a period of relative détente, including the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963) and later strategic arms limitation talks (SALT).
Candidates should weigh whether the crisis represented a genuine structural turning point toward more managed superpower competition, or merely a temporary de-escalation followed by renewed Cold War tension in later decades (e.g. Vietnam, Afghanistan).
Mark scheme guidance: top answers avoid treating the crisis as ending Cold War tension outright, correctly framing it as a significant but partial and temporary shift.
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Explain the reasons for, and consequences of, US involvement in the Vietnam War.
a:
Reasons: Cold War "domino theory" reasoning following the French withdrawal from Indochina (1954) and the division of Vietnam; escalation after the Gulf of Tonkin incident (1964).
Consequences: high casualties and use of controversial tactics (chemical defoliants, events such as the My Lai massacre) fuelled growing domestic anti-war opposition; US withdrawal (Paris Peace Accords, 1973) followed by communist reunification of Vietnam (1975); damaged US international prestige and domestic political trust, producing lasting caution in subsequent US foreign policy interventions.
Mark scheme guidance: candidates should link the war's conduct and outcome to its wider significance for later US Cold War strategy, not describe it as an isolated conflict.
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Assess the relative importance of internal Soviet weakness and external Western pressure in explaining the end of the Cold War (1989-1991).
a:
Internal factors: long-term Soviet economic stagnation and inefficiency, the costly Afghan war (from 1979), and Gorbachev's reforms (glasnost, perestroika) that, while intended to strengthen the system, instead accelerated its unravelling by permitting open criticism and weakening central economic control.
External factors: sustained Western military and economic competition (including the Reagan-era arms build-up) placed additional strain on Soviet resources; the fall of Soviet-aligned Eastern European governments (1989) and the fall of the Berlin Wall demonstrated the collapse of Soviet regional control, culminating in the Soviet Union's dissolution in December 1991.
Mark scheme guidance: candidates must explicitly weigh internal versus external factors rather than listing them separately, reaching a reasoned judgement on relative importance for the top band.
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: "Financial bankruptcy, rather than Enlightenment ideas, was the decisive cause of the outbreak of the French Revolution in 1789." Discuss. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Fiscal Crisis:** Seven Years' War & American War of Independence debts forced Louis XVI to summon the Estates-General when First/Second Estates refused tax reform; 1788 hailstorm bread riots sparked urban explosion [13 marks].
- **Ideological/Social Catalysts:** Montesquieu, Rousseau, and Voltaire delegitimised absolutism and feudal privilege, giving the Third Estate political vocabulary (Sieyès' *What is the Third Estate?*) to turn a fiscal deadlock into a constitutional revolution [12 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Assess the extent to which Napoleon Bonaparte was "the heir of the French Revolution" rather than its destroyer between 1799 and 1814. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Preserver (Heir):** Code Napoléon codified legal equality of men, abolished feudalism & serfdom across Europe, guaranteed careers open to talent (*la carrière ouverte aux talents*), and upheld peasant land gains [13 marks].
- **Destroyer:** Crowned himself Emperor (1804), curtailed press freedom (Fouché police censorship), reduced women's legal status, Concordat reconciled Church privilege, and dynastic nepotism replaced republican elections [12 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Account for the failure of the 1848 Revolutions across Germany, Italy, and the Habsburg Empire. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Internal Divisions:** Liberal middle-class constitutionalists feared radical working-class socialism (e.g., Paris June Days, Frankfurt Assembly debates) and abandoned revolutionary alliances [10 marks].
- **Royalist Military & Ethnic Friction:** Monarchs retained loyal peasant conscript armies (Windischgrätz, Radetzky); Habsburg court exploited Slav vs Magyar ethnic tensions; Piedmont lacked Great Power backing [15 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Compare the respective contributions of Camillo di Cavour and Giuseppe Garibaldi to the Unification of Italy (1848–1870). [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Cavour (Statecraft & Diplomacy):** Modernised Piedmont economy/army, allied with France at Plombières (1858) to expel Austria from Lombardy [10 marks].
- **Garibaldi (Popular Revolutionary Action):** Conquered Sicily & Naples with his 1,000 Red Shirts (1860), hand-delivering the South to Victor Emmanuel II to forge a single kingdom rather than Cavour's northern plan [10 marks].
- **External Factors:** Prussian victories in 1866 (Venetia) and 1870 (Rome) completed unification [5 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: "Bismarck succeeded in unifying Germany primarily through opportunistic diplomacy and Prussian economic might rather than a rigid long-term masterplan." Evaluate this judgement. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Intentionalist ("Blood & Iron") View:** Orchestrated 1864 Danish, 1866 Austro-Prussian, and 1870 Franco-Prussian wars systematically to isolate foes [10 marks].
- **Structuralist/Opportunist View (A.J.P. Taylor / Pflanze):** Exploited diplomatic mistakes by Napoleon III, British non-intervention, Zollverein customs union dominance, Moltke/Roon rail-rifle superiority, and reacted unpredictably to Ems Telegram opportunities [15 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Assess the responsibility of Germany and Austria-Hungary versus Russia and France for the outbreak of the First World War in August 1914. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Fritz Fischer Thesis (German Primacy):** "Blank cheque" to Vienna, naval arms race, Schlieffen Plan violating neutral Belgium, and desire for Mitteleuropa hegemony [11 marks].
- **Shared Responsibility (Christopher Clark / Joll):** Austria's reckless ultimatum to crush Serbia; Russia's premature general mobilisation; inflexible alliance commitments & French revanchism [14 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Evaluate the view that the Treaty of Versailles (1919) was a "fatally flawed compromise that neither crushed Germany permanently nor reconciled it to peace." [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Harshness fueling German Resentment:** Article 231 War Guilt, 6.6 billion GBP reparations, Alsace-Lorraine & Polish Corridor territorial losses, 100,000-man army cap, dictated *Diktat* [13 marks].
- **Incomplete Enforcement:** Left Germany's industrial core and population intact while US isolationism and Anglo-French disagreements left France insecure yet unable to enforce terms long-term [12 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Account for the failure of the League of Nations to preserve collective security during the 1930s. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Structural Weaknesses:** Absence of USA, USSR (until 1934), and departing aggressors (Japan, Germany, Italy); unanimity voting rule; no standing military force [11 marks].
- **Great Power Self-Interest (Manchuria 1931 & Abyssinia 1935):** Britain and France prioritised Depression budgets and Hoare-Laval realpolitik appeasement over credible oil/Suez sanctions, destroying collective security [14 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Assess the relative importance of Nazi terror and propaganda versus genuine economic recovery in explaining Hitler's consolidation of power in Germany between 1933 and 1939. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Consent & Economic Recovery:** Fall of unemployment from 6 million to near zero via Autobahnen, rearmament, KdF leisure schemes, and nationalist Versailles triumphs built real popular support [13 marks].
- **Coercion & Propaganda:** Gestapo/SS concentration camps (Dachau), Night of the Long Knives, Enabling Act, Gleichschaltung coordination of courts/schools, and Goebbels' mass media monopoly silenced all organised opposition [12 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Examine how the Marshall Plan (1947), Berlin Blockade (1948–49), and NATO turned Cold War ideological rivalry into permanent European division. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Economic & Geopolitical Containment:** Marshall Aid fused Western European recovery to US capitalism while Stalin banned satellite participation (Cominform/Comecon) [11 marks].
- **Military Crystallisation:** Western currency reform triggered Stalin's Berlin Blockade; the allied Airlift led directly to rival German states (FRG & GDR, 1949), NATO, and later the Warsaw Pact (1955) [14 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Evaluate the achievements and limitations of Bismarck's Alliance System (1871–1890) in maintaining European peace. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Objectives & Networks:** Aimed to isolate revanchist France and avert a two-front war via Dreikaiserbund, Dual Alliance (1879), Triple Alliance (1882), and Reinsurance Treaty (1887) [13 marks].
- **Inherent Contradictions:** Austro-Russian Balkan rivalry constantly strained the system, forcing secret incompatible commitments that collapsed once Wilhelm II dropped the Reinsurance Treaty in 1890 [12 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Compare the New Economic Policy (NEP, 1921) under Lenin with Stalin's First Five-Year Plans (1928–1932) in their economic and human impact on the Soviet Union. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **NEP (Tactical Retreat):** Replaced War Communism requisitioning with tax-in-kind and small private trade—revived peasant grain output and light industry, though ideological NEPmen inequalities triggered Scissors Crisis [11 marks].
- **Stalin's Command Revolution:** Forced collectivisation & dekulakisation devastated Ukraine/Kazakhstan (1932–33 famine) while rapid state heavy-industrialisation built Magnitogorsk steel & hydro power vital for WWII survival [14 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Account for the victory of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) over the Guomindang (KMT) in the Chinese Civil War (1946–1949). [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **CCP Strengths:** Yan'an peasant land reform, disciplined PLA guerrilla-to-conventional warfare, strict Eight Points of Attention morale, anti-Japanese patriotic prestige [13 marks].
- **KMT Weaknesses:** Chiang Kai-shek's hyperinflation, official corruption, brutal conscription, loss of urban middle-class support, and strategic overextension in Manchuria despite US aid [12 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History

q: Assess why the Civil Rights Movement in the United States achieved landmark legislative breakthroughs (1964 Civil Rights Act & 1965 Voting Rights Act) between 1954 and 1965. [25 marks]
a:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Grassroots Non-Violent Mobilisation:** Brown v Board (1954), Montgomery Bus Boycott, Greensboro sit-ins, Freedom Rides, Birmingham, and Selma exposed televised segregationist violence [13 marks].
- **Leadership & Political Context:** MLK Jr.'s moral coalition, SNCC/NAACP legal persistence, Cold War embarrassment pressuring JFK/LBJ, and Lyndon Johnson's congressional mastery (alongside growing urban militancy) [12 marks].
p: History A-Level Paper 2 — World and International History
